choices.text: Take the page and read it

ok.log: You take the page and read it; it is a laundry list, in a god's hand, with a drawing of a cat. {npc} laughs until they have to sit down.

fail.log: You take the page, and it is the true page, and it says that you lose. {npc} reads it over your shoulder and, mercifully, says nothing.

effects.log: You burn it unread, with {npc} watching. The smoke smells of cedar, and of something old and unfinished.

events.text: A dream-weaver of the Silent Hall sends you both the same dream, a long one, in which you share a cottage at the edge of a lake and argue about nothing. You wake with the smell of woodsmoke in your hair. {npc} appears at your door in the dawn with the same smell.

ok.log: You tell the dream aloud, and {npc} supplies the detail of the lake, and the two of you stand in the dawn laughing like fools.

fail.log: You tell the dream aloud and {npc} says "I did not have that part," and the moment closes, and you do not know which of you lied.

effects.log: You say nothing, and make breakfast, and {npc} washes up. It is the first meal you have ever shared.

events.text: {npc} comes to the foot of a mountain that is yours, sets down a bundle, and says, "It is every prayer I have received in an age that mentions you, by name. I have not answered one. I thought you might want them."

ok.log: You read the prayers and they are, mostly, kind. You answer three, and are surprised by the quality of the miracle; {npc} answers the rest.

fail.log: You read the prayers and they are not all kind. Some are curses, and some are worse: pleas that you came too late for. You sit with them a long while.

effects.log: You burn the prayers with {npc}, and the smoke goes down to the mortals, who feel a strange lightness and cannot say why.

events.text: A new god is born in the east, a tiny one, of a river-spirit and a thunder-cloud, and is carried to the Heavenly Court to be named. Both you and {npc} have been suggested as sponsors. The infant takes one look at you and one at {npc}, and begins to cry.

ok.log: You take the child first, and it stops crying, astonished, and is yours for the afternoon. {npc} makes faces over your shoulder.

fail.log: You take the child first and it howls. {npc} takes it, and it stops, and looks at you with an unfair expression.

effects.log: You hold the child together, one hand each, and the infant sleeps. It is named after the sound of the thunder.

events.text: {npc} is found sitting among the graves of the first mortals, in a field below the clouds, leaving a bowl of rice at each. "I do this every hundred years," {he} says. "I thought I should not be alone in it." There are ten thousand graves.

ok.log: You take half the field, with a bag of rice, and walk your rows. The work takes the day; the quiet lasts a long time after.

fail.log: You take half the field and run out of rice at the three-thousandth grave. {npc} hands you a second bag, uncomplaining.

effects.log: You walk the field beside them, bowl for bowl. At the last grave, {npc} leaves the bowl, and you leave a flower.

events.text: The Throne of Storms holds a feast and seats you and {npc} on opposite sides of a table forty yards long, so that you must shout. The feast is the loudest in memory, and by the third course you have both given up shouting, and are signalling.

ok.log: You win the signal game, a long hilarious pantomime that attracts half the hall; {npc} concedes by holding up both hands.

fail.log: You lose the signal game: {npc} understands your every gesture, and you understand none of theirs. The hall adores it.

choices.text: Walk round the table to them

effects.log: You walk round the table, forty yards, and sit beside {npc}, and the feast is quiet at last.

events.text: A shrine to a god of travellers stands on a crossroads, and the god has been gone for centuries; {npc} and you are the only gods who still visit it. This year the shrine bell rings by itself, and a small voice from the stones says: "Are you the ones?"

ok.log: You answer the voice, and it is a minor spirit, left behind, glad to be found; you both give it work, and a place at a feast.

fail.log: You answer the voice and it flees, afraid of your rank; {npc} sits down on the shrine step and calls it back, softly, until it comes.

effects.log: You leave a note on the step for the voice: "Come to the hall of the Green Assembly." {npc} adds a second line, and an address.

events.text: {npc} brings you a letter written in a mortal hand, from a village that prays to you both. It is a request: please settle your quarrel, because the people can no longer decide whom to thank for the rain. The villagers have all signed, with their thumbs.

ok.log: You reply with a miracle of rain and a note, plainly worded, and the village sings. {npc} adds a postscript that makes them cry.

fail.log: You reply with a miracle that is a little too loud; the village is delighted, and {npc} has to explain to the elders that it was a thunderclap, not an omen.

effects.log: You visit together, in disguise, as a pair of travelling peddlers, and eat bean soup with the elders, who pray for you without knowing.

events.text: At the Green Assembly, a very old god of the grove rises to say that the two of you are an old story with a bad ending, and that the Assembly would like to rewrite it. "There are rules," says the old god. "Choose a form: a play, a hymn, a feast."

ok.log: You choose the play and write your lines with {npc}, and the Assembly weeps at the last act; the story has a better ending than it deserved.

fail.log: You choose the play and forget your lines; {npc} covers for you in the ancient manner and the Assembly forgives you both.

effects.log: You choose the feast. {npc} brings the bread; you bring the wine. The Assembly eats it all and rewrites nothing.

events.text: A star goes out above the lower lands, and a mortal astronomer prays to the gods to know the reason. The one who answers is {npc}. When you appear, {npc} stands aside, makes room, and says: "You can answer. You have a better voice for bad news."

ok.log: You answer: the star was old, and tired, and went out gently. The astronomer takes it well, and writes it down. {npc} thanks you for the words.

fail.log: You answer, but the astronomer asks a second question you cannot answer; {npc} answers it for you, simply, in the mortal tongue.

effects.log: You ask {npc} to answer instead, and sit and listen. It is, as it turns out, a good answer.

events.text: The harvest god is to retire, and the Assembly proposes a tournament for the seat: a contest of fields. You and {npc} are the last two entered, and there is a single, difficult rule: each field must be sown by the other.

choices.text: Sow their field with your best seed

ok.log: You sow {npc}'s field with your best seed, and in the autumn it is the finest harvest of the age; {npc} sows yours with the same care, and the judges cannot choose.

fail.log: You sow their field in haste, and a late frost takes half of it; {npc} says it was theirs to lose and sows yours beautifully.

choices.text: Withdraw, and let them have the seat

effects.log: You withdraw and let {npc} take the seat. They decline it in the same breath. The old harvest god keeps the chair for another age.

events.text: {npc} arrives in the Hall of Echoes, where the prayers of the dead are kept, and says: "Our old names are in here, the ones we had when we were mortal. Together. I have a key." The key is made of bone and very old.

ok.log: You open the Hall. The names are there, two, on one slab, and the echo says them aloud. You do not remember them, and you cry anyway.

fail.log: You open the Hall and the echoes are too loud; you cannot hear the names, and {npc} can, and tells you what they are, softly.

effects.log: You leave the Hall locked. {npc} returns the key to its niche, and the two of you walk out through the rain without a word.

events.text: A new pantheon-day begins, and each god may ask one favour of the Will of Heaven. {npc} announces they will use theirs on you: "I ask that you be given whatever you most want." The court goes silent. The sun considers it.

ok.log: You say what you most want, honestly, and the sun nods, and {npc} listens with open face; the favour is granted in a form you did not expect.

fail.log: You cannot say what you most want. The sun waits. {npc} waits. At last you say "peace," and it comes out sounding like a lie, and is not.

effects.log: You ask the same favour of the sun for {npc}. The court holds its breath, and the sun laughs, a golden sound.

events.text: The sea-god's daughter is to marry, and both you and {npc} have been invited to bring a gift and a blessing. You arrive at the same time with the same gift, a pearl shaped like a tear, which neither of you has mentioned. The bride looks from one to the other.

ok.log: You offer yours with a toast, and the toast is good, and {npc} follows with a better one; the bride keeps both pearls.

fail.log: You offer yours with a toast and the toast goes wrong; {npc} rescues it with a joke, and the bride laughs, charmed.

effects.log: You offer to share a pearl, and {npc} agrees. The bride sets the two together in a ribbon.

events.text: There is an unspoken rule in the Divine Realm that gods do not visit each other's dreams unasked. {npc} is found at your bedside, in the dream-hours, apologising: "I could not wake you. You were in a nightmare. I wanted to see that you came out of it."

ok.log: You pretend you were awake and wave away the apology, and {npc} is both relieved and offended; the nightmare is, at last, the less of the two.

fail.log: You pretend you were awake and {npc} knows you were not, and says so, quietly; there is a silence you will remember.

effects.log: You thank them honestly, which you did not think you could. {npc} blinks, and nods, and goes.

events.text: The mountains of the Throne of Storms have a custom: two gods who disagree for an age must climb the highest peak together, roped, in silence. {npc} unrolls the rope on your doorstep and ties one end to their belt. "Tomorrow at dawn," they say.

ok.log: You lead the climb, and the ice does not trouble you, and at the summit you and {npc} look down at a world that is very small. You say a word. It is the first of the day.

fail.log: You lead the climb and fall; the rope holds, because {npc} holds it, and you hang above the abyss for a long second, and then you climb on.

effects.log: You follow them up, and the silence is easy, and at the summit {npc} hands you a flask. It is the best silence of your life.

events.text: A village of the lowlands has built a shrine that holds a statue of a god who is, by every sign, a blend of the two of you: your eyes, {npc}'s mouth, and a posture neither can place. The village prays to it earnestly. The statue is quite good.

choices.text: Bless the village as one god

ok.log: You bless the village as one god, in a voice not quite yours; {npc} adds their own, and the harvest that year is odd, shaped like neither of you.

fail.log: You bless the village as one god and the blessing does not take; the statue cracks, and {npc} mends it with a smile and a thumb.

choices.text: Leave the statue as it is

effects.log: You leave the statue as it is. In the years to come, it is the only likeness anyone thinks to compare you with.

events.text: On the evening of the Great Silence, when the gods do not answer prayers for a night, {npc} knocks at your door and says: "I do not want to be alone for it." You have never been asked this by anyone, divine or mortal. The night is long.

ok.log: You let them in and the two of you spend the night in the quiet, with tea and a candle, saying little. In the morning the prayers resume, and you are not ready.

fail.log: You let them in and cannot find a word to say; {npc} sits with you in the silence, patiently, and is a better guest than you were a host.

effects.log: You say that you cannot, tonight. {npc} nods, and goes, and you sit alone, regretting it, for most of an age.

events.text: {npc} has brought a drum, a plain skin drum from the lowlands, and is tapping a rhythm on it in the doorway of your temple. "I learned this from a mortal child," {he} says. "I thought you would like it." It is a very simple rhythm.

ok.log: You drum the answer back on the temple rail, and the rhythm catches. The two of you play for an hour, and the nearby clouds lean in.

fail.log: You drum the answer back and miss the beat; {npc} smiles and drums it again, slowly, until you have it.

effects.log: You sit and listen. It is a very simple rhythm, and you find you will remember it long after the drum is gone.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has decreed that every god must name a successor, or the domain will pass at the next age to the lot. {npc} comes to you in a state, with a list: eleven names, ten crossed out, and the last one is your name, in pencil.

choices.text: Write your own name on theirs

ok.log: You write your name on their list and they write theirs on yours, and the Court is baffled and the clerk accepts both.

fail.log: You write your name and {npc} crosses it out and writes another, an apprentice, and the apprentice is startlingly good.

effects.log: You burn the list. The Court will have to decide by lot, which is fair, and rather nice, and {npc} agrees.

events.text: {npc} comes to your altar at the end of a long age, and says: "I have been your enemy for lives. I would like to stop. If you wish it, I will lay down every claim. If you do not, I will understand." {He} holds out an open hand, palm up, as a mortal does when praying.

choices.text: Take their hand, and end it

effects.log: You take it. A sound like a great door closing, softly, in a far room. The knot between you does not break. It changes grain.
You refuse, and what follows is the last duel, and its winner is not the point. When it is over, the thing between you has a finish.
You ask for an age. {npc} nods, gravely, and gives it, and neither of you knows what you will answer.

events.text: The Silent Hall calls it the last audience, though nobody is sure why. {npc} comes without a weapon. "You choose," {he} says. "The last blow, or the first honest word."

effects.log: You say the honest word. It is two syllables. {npc} weeps, quietly, and so, you find, do you.
You strike, and it is clean, and it is over, and the Hall has never been so quiet. {npc} bows, once, and is gone.
You decline both. {npc} looks at you with a kind of fond exhaustion, and says, "As ever."

events.text: {npc} says that the knot between your souls is thin now, worn nearly through by use. {He} asks whether you would prefer to cut it, cleanly, or let it fray, and carry what is left, as a friend, for the rest of the ages.

choices.text: Let it be, and carry it

effects.log: You let it be. It frays slowly, and years later you find it has become something like a bridge.
You cut it. The silence afterwards is the cleanest you have ever heard, and the loneliest, and entirely your own.
You say neither. {npc} smiles, and the knot hums, and both of you pretend not to hear.

events.text: At the end of ten thousand years of dispute, {npc} comes to your altar and kneels. "I yield," {he} says. "Not because you are stronger. Because I am tired of being the thing that is never enough." {He} looks up. "Will you take it?"

effects.log: You raise them up, and say that there was never a contest, only two people, and it is the truest thing you have said. {npc} weeps.
You accept. The weight of it settles on you like snow. It is a victory and it is not at all what you wanted.
You decline to take it, and decline to give it back, and the matter stays unsettled, and warm.

events.text: You find {b3_legend} at the end of a corridor of the Divine Realm that is not on any plan, sitting perfectly still. They do not look up. The silence is of the kind that has been practised for ages, and is not, you realise, a rebuke.

effects.log: You sit. An hour passes, then an age. When you rise you have been taught something, though you could not say what.

choices.text: Ask the one question you have

effects.log: You ask. The answer is five words, and it will take you a thousand years to understand all of them.
You bow and go. The legend lifts one finger, perhaps a blessing, perhaps a fly. You will never know.

events.text: Every god has a story of {b3_legend}, and no two agree. You find them at a wayside altar of the lower sky, quite real, arguing mildly with a lamp about its brightness. The lamp is losing.

effects.log: You take the lamp's side. The legend is delighted, and the afternoon, which is three hundred years, is unexpectedly useful.

choices.text: Ask which of the stories is true

effects.log: "All of them," says the legend, "in their fashion. Pour me some more."
You fill the lamp. The legend accepts, with great seriousness, as if the filling were the point of the visit. Perhaps it was.

events.text: {b3_legend} sees you across a crowded hall of the Heavenly Court and crosses the room to you, ignoring three ministers of fate. "You," they say. "I have been meaning to look at you." They look for a very long time.

effects.log: You hold it. The look goes on, and on, and then ends, and the legend says only "Good", and leaves the ministers in your debt.
"A slow fuse," says the legend. "Lit." They are gone before you can ask more.
You bow low. The legend grunts. It is, as far as the Court can tell, an endorsement.

events.text: At the edge of the Divine Realm, {b3_legend} is dropping prayers over the side, one at a time, and listening. "There," they say, as you come up. "That one fell a long way. Did you hear?" You did not, but you listen.

effects.log: You drop one. The legend cocks its head. "Not bad," they say. "You have the ear for it."
"For when it stops," they say. "It never does. That is the secret. Do not tell the mortals."
You stand beside them. After an hour the legend sighs, contentedly, and you feel something in you set down a load.

events.text: The temple is empty and the door unbarred. Inside, {b3_legend} is sweeping a floor that looks as though it had never been dirty. They look up and say, "Thank goodness, someone to hold the other end," and hand you a broom.

effects.log: You sweep. It takes three days. At the end the legend inspects the floor, and nods, and you have the odd sense of having passed an examination.
"Because somebody must," says the legend, and leaves it at that, and it stays with you for ten thousand years.
You decline the broom, with an apology. The legend takes it and goes on sweeping, quite unoffended.

events.text: You meet {b3_legend} at a ferry landing on the river between the lower sky and the upper, both of you waiting for a boat that has not come in an age. They tell you it is coming, with such confidence that you begin to feel it too.

effects.log: You wait. Nothing arrives. But the waiting has a shape, and the shape is a lesson in patience that cannot be hurried.

choices.text: Ask what they are waiting for

effects.log: "For the next thing," they say. "It is always the next thing." You write it down, and cannot read it later.
You offer to row, and the legend laughs until they have to sit, and accepts, and you row the whole afternoon, round and round in sunlight.

events.text: {b3_legend} challenges you to a contest of silence, a strange match, with a single secret each as the stake. You are curious enough to accept. The contest lasts three days of the lower world, and a hundred years of yours.

choices.text: Hold the silence to the end

ok.log: You hold it, and in the end it is the legend who speaks first, and gives you the secret, kindly.

fail.log: You break first, and the legend takes your secret with a very gentle expression.

effects.log: You concede at once. The legend is a little disappointed, a little pleased, and tells you a smaller secret, as a consolation.
You offer a draw, and the legend, to the astonishment of three listening angels, accepts.

events.text: You find {b3_legend} asleep under a great tree in a small grove of the Green Assembly, snoring gently, and the tree is shedding petals over them. You are not sure whether to wake them. A single petal falls on your sleeve, and it is warm.

effects.log: The legend wakes, blinks, and says "Ah, you again," as if you had met every age. It is a pleasant lie, and you are not sure it is one.
You sit. The petals fall. When the legend wakes at last, you are a little calmer than you were.

choices.text: Leave a cup of water beside them

effects.log: You leave a cup. It is cold when they wake, and they drink it anyway, and the gesture is repaid in time.

events.text: The great gate of an unnamed shrine opens before you, and {b3_legend} stands in the court beyond, looking at the sky. "I have been told," they say, "that you are a god who gets to the point. Get to the point."

effects.log: You say it plainly. The legend nods, and tells you the one thing you needed, and a second, free of charge.

choices.text: Say you have come to learn

effects.log: You say you have come to learn. The legend sighs, "Ah. Everyone says that," and teaches you anyway.

choices.text: Say you only came to see

effects.log: You say you only came to see. The legend roars with laughter, and for the rest of the age you are a guest.

events.text: Rain, the first in a long age, falls on a tiny shrine at the edge of the Divine Realm, and {b3_legend} sits in the doorway, watching it with the look of someone seeing an old friend. They gesture you in, out of the wet.

choices.text: Sit in the doorway beside them

effects.log: You sit beside them. The rain falls for two days, and nothing is said, and it is the best conversation of your existence.

choices.text: Ask whether they remember a rain like it

effects.log: "There was one," says the legend, "and I was not the same after." That is all, and it is a great deal.
You go. The rain follows you down the steps for an hour, and then it clears.

events.text: At the lowest step of the heavens, {b3_legend} is picking up the small prayers that fall from above, one at a time, and putting them in a bag. "Somebody has to," they say. "They all come from somewhere."

effects.log: You help. The bag is heavy and the work slow, and when you finish the legend hands you a prayer, a plain one. It is warm.
"To the next step," says the legend. "Always to the next." You watch the prayers, and see them differently.
You offer a bigger bag. The legend looks at it, and at you, and says, "That is the first sensible thing anyone has said all age."

events.text: {b3_legend} has heard that you are said to have a sharp tongue, and asks for a demonstration, before an audience of nobody. You are not sure whether it is an invitation or a trap, but the legend waits, patient as a mountain.

ok.log: Your best is very good. The legend laughs, applauds, and tells three stories in return, each better.

fail.log: Your best falls flat, and the legend, kindly, pretends not to have heard.

effects.log: You decline. The legend nods, as if that were the real demonstration.
They give you theirs. It is one sentence. It is better than your best.

events.text: There is a story that {b3_legend} gives one gift to every god who passes, and you have come to see whether it is true. They are leaning on a gatepost, with a bag of small objects at their feet, and look you over with great care.

effects.log: You wait. They give you a smooth black stone, and tell you to keep it until it is of use. It is very heavy for its size.
You ask. The legend looks at you for a long time, and gives you what you asked, and something else you did not.
You offer a small plain thing of yours. The legend takes it with the care of a jeweller, and gives you a blessing in the first tongue.

events.text: {b3_legend} is judging a contest of lanterns lit by the faithful, far below, and has no idea they are the judge. They turn to you and ask which of the lanterns is best. A million hopeful mortals hold their breath.

effects.log: You choose with care, and the legend says you have chosen the same one as they would have, and gives you a warm, long look.
You pick the humblest. A child, below, bursts into tears of joy. The legend nods slowly, and writes something in the air.
You say all are best. The legend laughs, and the heavens laugh, and the lanterns rise, a million small suns.

events.text: You hear a piece of music from a closed room in the oldest part of the Silent Hall, and it is more beautiful than anything you have heard in ten thousand years. You open the door. {b3_legend} looks up from a battered instrument, and sets it aside, embarrassed.

effects.log: They play. It is not as good now they know you are listening, and then it is better, and then it is the best thing you have ever heard.
You apologise. The legend waves a hand. "It was only a tune," they say, and hums the last bar, and you will carry it for an age.
You ask. They say no, and teach you anyway, in the way that is not a lesson, for three weeks.

events.text: A prayer-angel finds you with a very odd summons: {b3_legend} wishes to see you, today, at noon, at a certain cloud. You go. The legend is there with a flask, a pair of cups, and the air of someone who has had a long, long walk.

effects.log: You sit, and pour the tea. The talk is of nothing, for hours, and the nothing is exact, and unforgettable.
"Because you were on the list," says the legend, mildly. "I am working through the list." It is a short answer and a long list.

choices.text: Accept the cup, and decline the flask

effects.log: You accept the cup, and decline the flask, and they say that is also the right answer.

events.text: A very old rumour says that {b3_legend} will lend a single blessing to anyone who can show a true scar. You have several. The legend, when found, wants to see all of them, and listens to each as though it were a hymn.

effects.log: You show them all. The legend is silent a long time, and then gives you a blessing so quiet you only notice it years later.
You show the oldest. The legend traces it with a finger and says it has healed well, and that is all, and it is enough.

choices.text: Show none, and tell the story instead

effects.log: You tell the story instead. The legend nods, "That is also a scar," they say, and you feel a great deal lighter.

events.text: Somebody tells you that {b3_legend} has been seen in the market of the lowest heaven, haggling, with the vigour of a young merchant, over a bag of dried plums. You go. It is true. They are winning.

effects.log: You help. The legend and you take the merchant for a good deal of plums, and share them on a wall, and it is a fine afternoon.
You haggle against them. It is a close fight, and a dear one, and the merchant goes home with a very good story.
You buy the plums. The legend takes them, solemnly, and bows. "I will remember the plums," they say. You hope so.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has asked {b3_legend} to give a lecture, and they have agreed, and when the day comes they stand at the lectern, look at the three hundred gods before them, and say, "I have nothing to say," and sit. The hall is silent. Then someone claps.

effects.log: You clap. The hall follows. The legend looks up, astonished, and then, very slowly, pleased.
You stay seated, and think about what had been said by not saying it. The thought will keep you busy for an age.
You go up. "That was the best lecture I have ever given," says the legend, softly. "Thank you for not asking what it was about."

events.text: You and {b3_legend} are the only two awake in the Divine Realm at the hour when no prayers come. The legend is awake because they never sleep. You are awake because you cannot. They offer you a bowl of something warm. It is delicious.

effects.log: You eat in silence. The bowl is warm, and the silence is wide, and when you are done you find the world is slightly less heavy.
"Soup," says the legend. "Mostly soup." You decide not to push.
"I am not awake," they say. "I am simply not asleep. There is a difference, and it is the whole of what I know."

events.text: When you reach {b3_legend}'s door, a notice is pinned to it: "Out. Back in an age. Please take a number." There are, truly, a great many numbers, curled on the hook, and the one on the top is yours.

effects.log: You take it. You wait. The age passes in small ways, and when the legend returns, you are still there, and the door opens.

choices.text: Take a number, and go away

effects.log: You take a number, and go, and put it on your shelf, and think of it on odd days with a warm, unfinished feeling.
You leave a note. Years later a reply arrives, one word. It is "Yes."

events.text: There is an old custom among the gods: to meet {b3_legend}, you must come with something to give and nothing to ask. You arrive with a loaf of plain bread, and the legend looks at it for a long time.

effects.log: The legend takes the bread, and eats it, slowly, and says it is the best they have had. It is not, but they mean it as a kind of blessing.

choices.text: Ask if they would like something else

effects.log: You ask. They say bread is the right thing, and you are the first to bring it in three thousand years.

choices.text: Keep the bread, and give nothing

effects.log: You keep the bread. The legend watches you, and says "Ah," in a tone that is not unkind, and does not say what it means.

events.text: A very small dispute, over the toll of one prayer at a bridge between two minor altars, has gone to {b3_legend} for judgement, and they have been hearing it for three days. They look at you, a passing god, and say, "You. You decide." Both parties turn.

effects.log: You rule for the toll-keeper. The traveller grumbles, pays, and then, at the last, grins. The legend nods, and says that is the kind of thing that makes a bridge.
You rule for the traveller. The toll-keeper takes it with grace, and the legend says, mildly, "Interesting."
You make them share. Both are unsatisfied. Both go away to tell it as a victory. The legend says that is the best kind of justice.

events.text: You find {b3_legend} in a garden of white stones, rearranging them with infinite care, one by one. Every so often they step back and look, and move one a hair to the left. You realise they have been doing this since before the first dawn.

effects.log: You move one. The legend considers it for a long time and moves it back, a hair to the right, and says, "Better." You do not see the difference. You will, in a thousand years.

choices.text: Ask what the garden is for

effects.log: "For being a garden," they say, without turning. "That is all any of us are for."
You sit and watch. You watch for three days. At the end of it, the garden looks the same, and you do not.

events.text: {b3_legend} stops you on the great stair, with a hand on your sleeve, and says, quite seriously: "You are about to make a mistake. A large one. I cannot say what. I only wanted to say that I will not think less of you."

effects.log: You thank them, and take extra care for an age, and the mistake, when it comes, is smaller than it would have been.
"I do not know," says the legend. "I am only old, not clever." You have never been so reassured.
You go on, regardless, and make the mistake, and the legend, when you next meet, says nothing about it, and that is the kindest thing.

events.text: Somebody has told {b3_legend} that you have been looking for them for centuries, and they have come to your altar, mildly annoyed, to find out why. They stand in the doorway, rained-on and sceptical, like a very old cat.

effects.log: You invite them in. They sit by the lamp, and say nothing, and drink three cups of water, and leave, and the room is warmer for it.
You ask. They answer in a dozen words, and turn to go, and then turn back and add a thirteenth, which is the one that matters.

choices.text: Say you have forgotten the question

effects.log: You say you have forgotten. They look at you for a long moment, and say, "Good. Then you are ready," and walk off, leaving you more confused than ever.

events.text: At a festival of lanterns in the oldest part of the Divine Realm, the crowd parts for {b3_legend} as for a ship, and the legend, spotting you at the edge, takes you by the sleeve and hauls you through, and says to the gods: "This one is with me."

effects.log: You go along. For a night you are a legend's guest, and the whole hall bows to you, and you are very, very careful where you put your feet.
"Wherever it gets interesting," says the legend, and leads you on, and it gets interesting.
You slip away. The legend does not seem to mind. At dawn, you find a lantern at your door, and a smile you cannot place.

events.text: {b3_legend} teaches a class at the lowest school of the heavens, for the children of newly risen gods, and has done for ten thousand years. They look up from a lesson on how to hold a brush and say, "Ah, a visitor. Good. You hold it. Show them."

effects.log: You show. The children watch, rapt, and the legend corrects your grip, mildly, in front of all of them. It is a very good lesson.

choices.text: Say you are not a teacher

effects.log: "No one is," says the legend. "Show them anyway." You do, and the children learn from your errors, which is the best kind.
You sit among them. It is a very small stool. You learn to hold a brush properly for the first time in ten thousand years.

events.text: You wake to find {b3_legend} sitting at the foot of your bed, quite unalarmed, looking at the wall. "I came to borrow a cup of water," they say. "And then I forgot why I came, and have been sitting here, thinking. Do you mind?"

effects.log: You fetch water. They sip it, and say it is nearly as good as the water they came for, and tell you three things you did not know.

choices.text: Ask what they are thinking about

effects.log: "About whether to go on," they say, so simply that you almost miss it. You find you have a great deal to say.

choices.text: Go back to sleep, and let them be

effects.log: You go back to sleep. In the morning they are gone, and a full cup sits cooling on the table, and a faint warmth in it.

events.text: {b3_legend} stands at the bottom of a great well in the middle of a shrine and calls up to you: "Lower me a rope, or leave. I will not be lectured about my choices." You look down. They are not, in fact, in any danger. They are reading.

effects.log: You lower it. They tie a book to the end and ask you to read it aloud. It is very long, and you read it all.
"Myself," says the legend, from the dark. "A very old edition. It has some errors."
You leave. Years later you find a book on your table, tied with a rope, and an inscription in a very old hand.

events.text: The one the Book of Fates has knotted to you has had a bad age, and you know it the way you know the weather. A messenger would say it was nothing to do with you. Something in you says it is. You find yourself sending a small offering, without a name.

effects.log: You send it. It is received, and traced, and neither of you mentions it, and the knot between you hums quietly.
You hold it back. The pride is old and the habit older. You will think of it at altars, for a long time.

choices.text: Send it with your name on it

effects.log: You send it with your name. The reply is three lines, and the third is a joke, which is the best thing it could have been.

events.text: There is a god of the Silent Hall who looks at you sometimes as if you were a word on the tip of their tongue. You have the same feeling in return. Neither of you has ever spoken of it. Tonight, for no reason, you find yourself saying hello.

effects.log: You say hello properly. It is the beginning of a conversation that will last, on and off, for several ages.
You nod and go on. It is very correct, and it is a small, odd grief.

choices.text: Ask if they, too, feel it

effects.log: You ask. They look at you with huge, startled eyes, and say "Yes."

events.text: You wake with a name in your mouth that you do not know, and by the end of the day you learn that someone with that name has been raised a rank, and that you are, to your shame, rather jealous. You do not know the god. You are quite sure you know them.

effects.log: You send it. The reply comes by return, and says only: "Thank you. I felt that."
You work harder, for no reason you can name, and in the morning you are a little better than you were.
You pretend. It is a very poor pretence, and you carry it all week.

events.text: A seer of the Silent Hall says, without being asked, that you and someone you have not yet met are "an old hymn sung in two keys". You ask who. The seer cannot say. She only says to be kind, when the time comes.

effects.log: You promise. The seer looks relieved, and rather sad, and gives you a very small coin, for luck.

choices.text: Ask what happens if you are not

effects.log: "Then you will do it again, in the next life," she says. "It is the only rule."

choices.text: Say you do not believe in hymns

effects.log: You say so, loudly. The seer smiles, very kindly, as one smiles at a child.

events.text: The old unaccountable ache has come back, the one that surfaces in the week of the autumn offerings: that someone is behind you on the stair, a step back, and has been for lives. You turn. There is nobody. There is a lantern, still swinging.

effects.log: You wait. For an hour, then two. Nobody comes. But the waiting is a small warm thing, and you carry it home.
You walk on faster. Behind you the lantern swings, and the stair, for a moment, seems to hold its breath.

choices.text: Call out a name you do not know

effects.log: You call a name. The wind brings it back to you. It is, you realise, your own, in somebody else's voice.

events.text: In the middle of a feast of the twelve domains you have a sense that the one whose fate follows yours is in the room, and you scan every face. A stranger at the far end meets your eyes and holds them. Neither of you looks away for a very long time.

effects.log: You cross the room. It takes a long time, and a great deal of nerve, and at the end there is a very ordinary introduction, and a very unordinary silence.
You raise your cup. They raise theirs. That is all. It is a great deal.
You look away. It is a small cowardice, and you will remember it, and the next time you meet, you will not.

events.text: Someone leaves a white flower on your altar in the night, every year, on the same night. You have never seen them. This year you wait up, and in the small hours a shadow comes, and stops, and sees you, and does not run.

effects.log: You say it. The shadow says "You are welcome," and then, rather quietly, "You always say that."
"I do not know," says the shadow. "I only know that I have to." It is, you realise, the truest answer you have heard.
You offer. They sit, awkwardly, in the one good chair, and the two of you are quiet for a very long time.

events.text: When you were new to godhood, a stranger on the great stair said, "I will see you again, whatever happens." You had forgotten. Today, in a corridor of the Heavenly Court, a pair of eyes meet yours, and a voice from long ago says, softly, "There."

choices.text: Answer, as if you had been waiting

effects.log: You answer. It is the only thing you can do, and it is entirely right, and the rest of the age is never quite the same.
You say you do not. The stranger says, "No. But I will wait." It is an unkind kind of kindness.
You walk past, and your hands do not stop shaking until midnight.

events.text: A prayer reaches you that is not for your domain at all: a mortal asking, in a village you cannot place, that two people, a long way apart, might at last stop being enemies. There is no name on it. You feel it land in your chest like a stone in a pond.

choices.text: Answer it, as best you can

effects.log: You answer it, with a small, quiet nudge toward peace, and the village below sleeps a little easier, and you do not know why you wept.

choices.text: Pass it to the Silent Hall

effects.log: You pass it to the Hall. The Hall, which never replies, replies: a single page, folded, which you do not open.
You keep it as your own prayer, and say it, now and then, in the evening, without being sure who you are saying it to.

events.text: You dream of a battlefield you do not recognise, and a figure on the far side of it, and the dream ends in a long look rather than a blow. You wake with the strong sense that it was a memory. At the Court the next day, someone looks at you with the same face.

effects.log: You say it. They go white, then pink, and say: "So did I. For a hundred years."
You say nothing. They say nothing. The silence at the Court is, for a day, the most interesting event in the Divine Realm.

choices.text: Look it up in the Book of Fates

effects.log: You look it up. The page is blank where it should not be, which is an answer of a kind.

events.text: There is a song the mortals sing in one valley of the lower world, about two stars that follow each other round the sky and never quite meet. You find yourself humming it at your altar. Somewhere nearby, someone is humming the other part.

effects.log: You hum along. A harmony forms, from nowhere, between two altars, and the mortals below look up, and wonder, and sing louder.
You follow the other voice. It leads you in circles, and then to a door, and then to a god you almost know.
You stop. The other voice goes on a moment, uncertain, and then stops too. It is the shyest conversation in the heavens.

events.text: A messenger from a distant domain arrives with a small box and no name. In it is a hairpin, a plain one, and a note: "You will not remember this. Keep it. I am told it was yours." Whoever sent it signs with a single, hopeful ink-drop.

effects.log: You keep it, and wear it, and feel an odd rightness, as if a sentence had been completed after a very long pause.

choices.text: Send it back with a question

effects.log: You send it back with a question. The answer comes in a year: "I do not know. I only know it is yours."
You put it in the vaults of your domain, with a small label, and visit it, from time to time, when no one is looking.

events.text: At the foot of the great altar of your domain you find a child's toy, a small wooden horse, left by a pilgrim. It is not a gift for you. A scribble on the base says "for the other one". You do not know what the other one is. You are quite sure you do.

choices.text: Carry it to the one it is meant for

effects.log: You carry it across the heavens to an altar not your own. The god who receives it holds it for a long time and says only, "Thank you. I lost it a long way back."
You leave it. In the morning it is gone, and a small clean space is left on the altar, and you feel oddly accompanied.
You keep it on your shelf, and talk to it now and then, in the evenings, in a voice you do not use for anything else.

events.text: While a famine of belief moved across the lower lands, {b3_rival} has taught a flock of sparrows in your valley to chirp in the cadence of your name, slightly sarcastically. The valley finds the birds charming. You have been a god long enough to know when a barb is a barb.

ok.log: By dusk the whole flock answers {b3_rival}'s birds in a descant, and the valley decides which side it likes better.

fail.log: The sparrows learn only the first half of the reply, and {b3_rival} has the rest of the evening to finish it for them.

choices.text: Send {b3_rival} a cage of owls, with thanks

effects.log: The owls arrive with a card thanking {b3_rival} for the lesson in tone. They are said to be still discussing it.

choices.text: Leave the sparrows to their song

effects.log: You let the birds chirp. By the second season the valley has stopped hearing sarcasm and only hears you, which is a kind of fame.

events.text: Under a sky you had both made, and could not quite agree on, Your shrine in the eastern valley is found swept and the roof patched, with the work signed in a small, resigned hand that you know from the Throne of Storms. Neither of you refers to it again.

choices.text: Patch their roof in return, unsigned

effects.log: You mend the roof of {b3_rival}'s border shrine the same way, in the dark, and leave the nails very slightly crooked on purpose.

choices.text: Sign your thanks in the same hand

ok.log: You sign a thank-you in a small resigned hand of your own, and {b3_rival} pins it where the pilgrims can read it.

fail.log: Your thanks comes out stiff, and {b3_rival} files it with the rest.

choices.text: Say nothing, and keep the roof dry

effects.log: You let the roof keep out the rain, and the eastern valley notices only that the rain has stopped coming in.

events.text: In the court of the gods, in the slow part of the afternoon, {b3_rival} and you have both been named in a mortal prophecy as the one who will bless the new bridge-city, and the city has asked, politely, for a demonstration. You can hear the clouds thinking about it.

choices.text: Demonstrate with a single, perfect blessing

ok.log: Your blessing lies across the bridge-city like a warm hand, and the mortals ask you to stay.

fail.log: Your blessing comes a half-beat after {b3_rival}'s, and the city thanks you for trying.

effects.log: You propose a joint blessing, and the city, flattered, agrees. {b3_rival} agrees with a speed that suggests they had thought of it first.

choices.text: Let the city choose by lot

effects.log: You let the city draw lots, and the lot falls where it falls, and you bear it with a good grace the clouds applaud.

events.text: At the turning of an age, in the court of the gods, a new temple on the plain is dedicated to "the god who stilled the river". You stilled it. The inscription is in {b3_rival}'s favourite typeface. You compose three replies and send none.

choices.text: Petition the temple for a correction

ok.log: Your petition cites the river's own silt record, and a new line is cut beneath the old one, in smaller letters but in your name.

fail.log: The temple clerks find your petition unfiled, and the inscription stays.

choices.text: Ask {b3_rival} to correct it in person

effects.log: You send {b3_rival} a polite note with a diagram of the river, and they appear at the temple in a plain cloak with a chisel.

choices.text: Still the river a second time

effects.log: You still the river again the next spring, in front of the whole plain, and let the water sign for you.

events.text: At the feast of the twelve domains, three thousand years into the dispute, a mortal city prays so loudly to both of you at once that the prayers collapse into a single scream; {b3_rival} turns and says, "I take the north half." You take the south. No other god is watching, which is a relief and a loss.

choices.text: Take the south half, and hold it

ok.log: You take the south with your whole domain behind you, and the city's scream becomes a murmur by dawn.

fail.log: The south slips through your hands for a breath before you catch it.

choices.text: Take the north, and give {b3_rival} the south

effects.log: You swap halves with {b3_rival} at the last second on a hunch, and their face has the look of an old friend's.

choices.text: Stay out of the scream, answer one word

effects.log: You answer the city with one word, a name, and the scream settles into words again.

events.text: During a very long recess of the Book of Fates, you find {b3_rival} alone at the foot of a dead god's altar, replacing the candles, and they ask you for a light as though it were an ordinary request. You do not mention it afterwards, either of you.

choices.text: Hold the candles while they light them

effects.log: You hold the candles, and they light them one by one from your own small flame, and neither of you says whose altar it is.

ok.log: {b3_rival} tells you, after a long moment, a name you thought was forgotten, and you both say it once, aloud.

fail.log: {b3_rival} says it does not matter any more, and the candles burn on in silence.

effects.log: You give the light and go, and are the only witness of an act that will not be written in any book.

events.text: In the cold light of a star that neither of you had made, the priest of your oldest shrine, a man of seventy years, has been seen at {b3_rival}'s temple, praying with a face you do not recognise. It is not theft. It is simply taking.

choices.text: Go and ask the priest to supper

effects.log: You ask your old priest to supper, and he comes, embarrassed, and eats three helpings, and says nothing of the other temple.

choices.text: Pray at the other temple for a day

ok.log: You kneel in {b3_rival}'s temple for a day and pray your priest's prayer, and the old man finds you at dusk and weeps.

fail.log: You are noticed at once and escorted out with great courtesy.

choices.text: Release him from his long service

effects.log: You release him with a blessing from the shrine's last step, and he goes where his knees prefer, and your oldest shrine is quiet.

events.text: In the weeks after an unexpected miracle, whose credit was unclear, {b3_rival} is named the god of a new domain, the Mist, which the Heavenly Court has been reluctant to create. The lamps burn late on their mountain. It is a long time since anyone but them mattered this much.

effects.log: You send {b3_rival} a letter written in condensation, which fades as it is read, and they keep the envelope.

choices.text: Visit the new domain's first rite

ok.log: You visit the first rite of the Mist and are the one guest the new god cannot look at without smiling.

fail.log: You arrive when the fog is thickest and are lost in it for an hour.

choices.text: Watch the lamps burn from your own mountain

effects.log: You watch the lamps burn on their mountain till the small hours, and go to bed a little taller for having had the neighbour.

events.text: On the night the worshippers lit the great fires far below, {b3_rival} issues a formal challenge to a contest of rains over a dry field, with the farmers acting as judges. The farmers are delighted and wholly impartial. You feel very old, and very young.

ok.log: Your rain falls on the farmers' field in a clean silver sheet, and the farmers, impartial, drown in applause.

fail.log: Your rain is thin as breath, and {b3_rival}'s soaks the field.

choices.text: Share the rain between two halves

effects.log: You and {b3_rival} each rain on half the field, and the farmers, who wanted neither to win, give you both a loaf.

choices.text: Let the farmers judge by the crop

effects.log: You let the farmers judge by the crop at harvest, and the contest is settled by wheat, which is the better court.

events.text: At the feast of the Harvest, {b3_rival} raises a cup "to the gods who did what they could", and looks, for a long moment, in the direction of your table. You will remember this for a thousand years.

choices.text: Raise your own cup to the same toast

effects.log: You raise your cup to the gods who did what they could, and let the grove decide who was more thoroughly toasted.

choices.text: Name what you could, and did

ok.log: You list your doings in a voice so level that the old trees lean in, and {b3_rival} sits down with a face like a closed book.

fail.log: The list is accurate and long, and the grove has heard enough lists to last it a thousand years.

choices.text: Eat your supper and remember it

effects.log: You finish the feast without a glance in their direction, and put the toast away with all the others you will repay in due time.

events.text: A few centuries after the last time you had both said "never again", the prayers of your coast, held up for a year by a clerk of the Silent Hall, arrive in a bundle with {b3_rival}'s seal on the string and nothing else. It changes nothing and everything.

choices.text: Answer the coast's prayers first, and fast

effects.log: You work through the bundle that night, every prayer answered, and send the string back with a knot in it for {b3_rival}.

choices.text: Ask the clerk what was said

ok.log: The clerk, pleased to be asked, admits {b3_rival} never said a word, only waited, and the fact is worth a good deal.

fail.log: The clerk grows wary and says it was an ordinary delay.

choices.text: Keep the seal and the string

effects.log: You keep the seal and the string and drop both in a drawer, to be understood later.

events.text: At a convocation of domains called to discuss, supposedly, something else, the god of Beasts has offered a golden horn to whoever calls the first herd to water this spring. {b3_rival} has been out since before dawn. It is a small thing and the stakes are everything.

choices.text: Call the first herd at dawn

ok.log: The herd comes to your call before {b3_rival} has finished tying the second knot, and the god of Beasts hands you the horn.

fail.log: The herd lingers on the hill and goes to {b3_rival}'s side of the water.

choices.text: Ask the beasts what they want

effects.log: You ask the beasts what they want, and a lame old stag leads the herd to the spring in the middle, where you and {b3_rival} arrive together.
You sleep until noon and walk to the spring at your own pace, and the horn goes where it goes.

events.text: When the prayers came in like weather, all from one side of the world, {b3_rival} is hailed in a mortal festival as the originator of the tradition of lamp-floating. It was a village girl, and then you, and then nobody remembered. Faith is a slow court.

effects.log: You trace the girl's line to a baker's family in the lowlands and tell them whose idea it was, and the baker cries over the flour.

choices.text: Float the first lamp of the year yourself

ok.log: You float the first lamp at the festival, and the crowd falls so quiet that you can hear the wick.

fail.log: Your lamp sinks near the shore, and the crowd politely looks at {b3_rival}.

choices.text: Let the tradition keep its own story

effects.log: You let the festival keep its confusion, because a lamp floats just as well whoever started it.

events.text: In a quiet corner of the Silent Hall, where no one is allowed to raise a voice, a bridge of rainbow that links the Sea to the Mountains is failing, with a convoy of minor gods halfway across. {b3_rival} is already out on it. Whatever happens, it will not be spoken of afterward.

choices.text: Run out on the bridge after {b3_rival}

ok.log: You reach the failing span as {b3_rival} lowers the last minor god to safety, and the bridge goes down behind you both in a ribbon.

fail.log: A strand of the bridge gives under you, and {b3_rival} hauls you over by the collar.

choices.text: Hold the far anchor from the Mountains

effects.log: You take the Mountain end of the rainbow and hold it with your entire domain, and the bridge sags but does not fail.

choices.text: Wait on the shore and catch whoever falls

effects.log: You stand on the Sea bank with your cloak spread and catch whoever the rainbow lets go.

events.text: In the hour when mortals bring their offerings and the gods pretend not to count, a prayer reaches you meant for {b3_rival}, from a woman who forgot the god's name and addressed it "the other one". You forward it. {b3_rival} reads it, and is quiet. You notice you are not angry.

choices.text: Forward it with a note of your own

effects.log: You forward the prayer with a line: 'She says you are the other one. She means well.' {b3_rival} reads both and is quiet longer.

ok.log: You answer the woman's prayer in {b3_rival}'s name, and she weeps and thanks 'the other one', and you both hear of it.

fail.log: Your answer lands in the wrong field, and the woman prays again, harder.

effects.log: You put the prayer away unopened, and the world below goes on addressing the wrong god kindly.

events.text: As the last of an age of worship burned down to its embers, the best of your angels of the harvest has been offered a seat in {b3_rival}'s choir, with the right to sing the solo, and has accepted with a sheepish bow. You have your own habits to blame.

choices.text: Offer a solo of your own

ok.log: You write the angel a solo that the Choir cannot match, and she sings it at the harvest, and returns.

fail.log: Your solo is too difficult, and she stays with {b3_rival}'s choir.

effects.log: You attend the harvest concert in {b3_rival}'s hall and applaud her solo first, loudly, and the angel's wings shake a little.

choices.text: Wish her well and promote the next

effects.log: You wish her well and make a younger angel the first voice of the harvest, and the choir is the better for a new throat.

events.text: At the edge of the divine realm, where the clouds are thinner and the prayers are louder, you are asked to give the dedication at the opening of a new temple of the Sky, and {b3_rival} is the first to applaud, and the last to leave. The ladder only goes one way, and every god is on it.

choices.text: Give the dedication, and thank {b3_rival} in it

effects.log: You thank {b3_rival} in the dedication by name and call them the one who made the ladder worth climbing, and the temple rings.

choices.text: Give the dedication in one sentence

ok.log: Your dedication is a single sentence of eleven words, and the Sky temple remembers it better than the hymn.

fail.log: Your dedication is so short that the crowd waits for the rest.

choices.text: Applaud last, and leave the dedication to others

effects.log: You applaud last, as befits a guest, and leave the dedication to the new priests.

events.text: Between two harvests, in the lull when the faithful are too busy to pray, the god of War declares a tourney of the minor gods, and {b3_rival} puts forward your name as a champion of "the other side", without asking you. The court is quieter than usual.

ok.log: You step into the lists as the champion of 'the other side' and make the god of War explain the title.

fail.log: You step in unready, and are put down by a very small god.

effects.log: You name {b3_rival} your second, to their astonishment, and the court's quiet turns to confused delight.

choices.text: Withdraw your name, with an excuse

effects.log: You withdraw your name with an excuse so elaborate that the god of War is persuaded and relieved.

events.text: On the steps of the Will of Heaven, in full sight of everyone, a mortal poet asks {b3_rival} which of the lesser gods best embodies patience. {b3_rival} names a snail, and then, warmly, you. All the gods are looking at you to see how you take it.

effects.log: You thank them warmly, and ask the poet to record that the snail got to the steps first. The crowd laughs, and not at you.

ok.log: You stand perfectly still until the mortal poet, flustered, writes your patience into the verse in full.

fail.log: You stand still so long that the poet leaves, and no verse is made at all.

choices.text: Climb past them at your own pace

effects.log: You go up the steps at a snail's pace, exactly, and nobody on them can say that you have not been patient.

events.text: At the funeral of a minor god, to which both of you were obliged to go, a famine god, sent against your fields by a stranger, finds {b3_rival} at the edge of the wheat, sitting on a fence, and they talk for a night. The famine goes elsewhere. You owe them now, and both of you know it.

choices.text: Sit on the fence with them

effects.log: You climb the fence beside {b3_rival}, say you heard it went well, and are told it did. Neither of you says by whose hand.

choices.text: Thank them in front of your priests

ok.log: You thank {b3_rival} aloud before the wheat-priests, and the whole field remembers whose fence it was.

fail.log: Your priests hear the thanks as a defeat, and mutter.

choices.text: Pay the debt privately, in grain

effects.log: You send grain to their coast with no label, and consider the account a little less lopsided.

events.text: On the mountain where the gods go when they want to be alone together, a mortal queen, deciding which temple to endow, invites you and {b3_rival} to speak at her table, one after the other, with a pause for soup between. The other gods are watching with a kind of bored interest.

ok.log: You speak after the soup, plainly, and the queen forgets her temple budget for a quarter of an hour.

fail.log: You speak after the soup and she has stopped listening.

choices.text: Praise {b3_rival}'s temple at your own turn

effects.log: You praise {b3_rival}'s works at your own turn, with details, and the queen, nonplussed, endows both.

choices.text: Eat the soup and say little

effects.log: You eat the soup, say little, and let the queen guess whom she would rather have at her table.

events.text: In a miracle-play at the great shrine, the god who descends in a golden chariot is made up to resemble {b3_rival}, and the chariot is the one you rode. The record is dry, which is the worst of it.

choices.text: Take the chariot and ride it onstage

ok.log: You ride the real chariot through the play's second act, and the audience sees both gods, one painted and one true.

fail.log: The chariot slips a wheel and the play ends in confusion.

effects.log: You send a word of praise for the costume to {b3_rival}, and the make-up artist is dismissed on a point of honour.

choices.text: Read the record, and put it down

effects.log: You read the dry record to the end and put it down. The play is only a play, and the chariot's wheels remember the road.

events.text: While a famine of belief moved across the lower lands, the sleeping god of the Harvest turns over in his dream, and the land tilts; you and {b3_rival} are the only two gods awake who know the old lullaby. You are, for one night, simply on the same side.

effects.log: You and {b3_rival} sing in unison, flat in the same places, and the land settles under you both, rocking.

choices.text: Take the verse they have forgotten

ok.log: You remember the second verse that {b3_rival} has lost, and the Harvest god sighs, and the land is still.

fail.log: You sing a second verse that belongs to another lullaby, and the land shifts.

effects.log: You keep the night watch on the hills while the lullaby is sung elsewhere, and are the first to see the dawn.

events.text: In the dream-hours, {b3_rival} is found by you in a small room with a window, looking at a field they used to own. Neither of you says that you have seen. It is the most honest hour of your acquaintance.

choices.text: Sit in the window with them

effects.log: You come to the window and look at the field without a word, and the field, which belongs to neither of you now, lets you.

ok.log: You name the crop the field used to bear, and {b3_rival} turns and says it was barley, and tells you the rest.

fail.log: You name the wrong crop, and {b3_rival} laughs for the first time in ages.

choices.text: Close the door, softly, and go

effects.log: You close the door and go, and the small room keeps what it keeps.

events.text: In the court of the gods, in the slow part of the afternoon, a wandering bard, who made your name in four kingdoms, now sings a new ballad about {b3_rival}, and when asked why, says it is a better rhyme. You feel the ground move, if there were ground.

choices.text: Commission a ballad from the bard

effects.log: You commission a ballad, and the bard, flattered, sings it in four kingdoms, and the rhyme is worse than {b3_rival}'s but the sentiment better.

choices.text: Duet with the bard in a tavern

ok.log: You turn up at a tavern in a plain hat and sing the chorus, and the room cannot tell which god it is cheering.

fail.log: You come in on the wrong verse, and the bard stops the song.

choices.text: Thank the bard for the four kingdoms

effects.log: You thank the bard for the four kingdoms and let the new ballad run its course.

events.text: At the turning of an age, in the court of the gods, the Book of Fates adds a line to {b3_rival}'s entry that you have never seen added to anyone's: a footnote, in the Hall's own hand, that says "Remarkable." Whatever the court says, the two of you know.

effects.log: You ask the Hall for the footnote, and a clerk fetches it, and you read the one word and, for a moment, say nothing.

choices.text: Earn a footnote of your own

ok.log: Your argument before the Hall gets its footnote at last, and the word is 'Noted.' It will do.

fail.log: Your argument gets no footnote at all, and the clerk apologises.

choices.text: Raise a cup to the word

effects.log: You raise a cup to the word 'Remarkable' at dinner, and the table does the same, without being sure which of you it is for.

events.text: At the feast of the twelve domains, three thousand years into the dispute, a bout of arm-wrestling between you and {b3_rival} over a keg of mortal ale has become a matter of honour for three pantheons, and a cloud-bank of onlookers has gathered. Someone is already laying odds, and you will not look.

ok.log: You pin {b3_rival}'s hand to the cloud-table at last, after an hour and a half, and three pantheons shout.

fail.log: Your arm gives at the last, and the keg is {b3_rival}'s, and the shout goes the other way.

choices.text: Declare the keg a shared prize

effects.log: You split the keg with {b3_rival} before the pantheons and pour it out together to the draw, and the odds are paid to the bookmakers.
You cheer for {b3_rival} in the open, to everyone's surprise, and watch the match from a good seat.

events.text: During a very long recess of the Book of Fates, the Silent Hall seats the gods of the dream and the dead by seniority. {b3_rival}, who has just been moved up a row, sends a cushion back for your bench, with a kind note. The court is not sure whether to laugh.

effects.log: You sit on it with a sigh of deep comfort, and the Silent Hall is left unsure which of you has been outwitted.

choices.text: Return it with a longer note

ok.log: Your note is so much kinder and so much more exact that the Hall passes it round, and {b3_rival} reads it twice.

fail.log: Your note is too long to be kind, and the Hall reads it as a sulk.

choices.text: Say nothing and keep your row

effects.log: You keep your bench and leave the cushion where it fell, and the recess goes on in a silence that favours the senior.

events.text: In the cold light of a star that neither of you had made, the sick animal in your temple, a ram of the old line, is looked after by one of {b3_rival}'s healers, and is cured. The healer left before you could ask. Gods have long memories, and this one will be kept.

effects.log: You send the healer the ram's first fleece, and a message that will be read by {b3_rival} before it reaches anyone else.

choices.text: Learn the cure the healer used

ok.log: You trace the healing to a tincture of rain-moss, and the ram's whole line prospers under your care.

fail.log: The cure leaves no trace you can follow, and the ram's lamb is never as strong.

choices.text: Keep the ram, and keep quiet

effects.log: You keep the ram in its stall, grateful in a quiet way that has no name in the Book of Fates.

events.text: In the weeks after an unexpected miracle, whose credit was unclear, There is a dispute over who gave the first lightning to the plains, and the Throne of Storms has sent a referee: a very young thunder-spirit with a clipboard. You would rather win than be right.

choices.text: Argue the first lightning from the records

ok.log: Your records, produced in the right order, decide the matter in an afternoon, and the thunder-spirit writes it down twice.

fail.log: Your records are in the wrong order, and the thunder-spirit asks for a recess.

effects.log: You call {b3_rival} as a witness, and they, caught between honesty and ambition, honestly confirm half of your story.

choices.text: Let the plains keep the lightning

effects.log: You let the plains keep the lightning, and the dispute is filed under the weather, where it belongs.

events.text: On the night the worshippers lit the great fires far below, a scholar of the lower world publishes a treatise on the gods and credits {b3_rival} with "the mercy of the spring", a mercy that was yours and dated. You have the facts, and they have the room.

choices.text: Write to the scholar, with dates

effects.log: You write a short, dated letter to the scholar, and a corrected edition appears in the lower world before the year is out.

choices.text: Ask {b3_rival} to confirm the facts publicly

ok.log: {b3_rival} confirms the mercy was yours in a short and unadorned statement that is copied in every temple.

fail.log: {b3_rival} confirms it with a careful vagueness that helps no one.

effects.log: You leave the scholar his error. The spring runs the same, and the lower world will correct itself in a generation.

events.text: In the Green Assembly's oldest grove, where the trees remember every oath, a lightning-storm wanders away from the Throne of Storms and settles on a village of your faithful; {b3_rival} arrives with a long rod and a prayer. There will be no one to witness, and so it will matter.

ok.log: You take the long rod and ground the storm into the earth, and the village stands.

fail.log: The storm throws you down, and {b3_rival} takes the rod back.

choices.text: Pray beside them, with your people

effects.log: You and {b3_rival} kneel with the village and send one prayer between you, and the storm, moved or tired, drifts away.

choices.text: Get the villagers to the cellars

effects.log: You get the village to the cellars and count them twice, and the storm passes over a street without a soul.

events.text: A few centuries after the last time you had both said "never again", {b3_rival} sends you a recipe, in a god's tongue, for the broth their mortal nurse made them when they were small, if gods are small. It reads, "For colds." For a moment the dispute is only an old habit.

choices.text: Make the broth and send a bowl

effects.log: You make the broth to the letter, and it takes you three tries, and you send {b3_rival} a bowl, with a note that says 'for colds'.

choices.text: Improve the recipe, and tell them

ok.log: You add a herb to the broth, and write back to say so, and {b3_rival} says the new one is better, and is sorry to say it.

fail.log: Your herb ruins the broth, and the correspondence goes on regardless.

choices.text: Keep the recipe and say nothing

effects.log: You keep the recipe in a drawer with the others and have the broth on a cold night, alone, in your own good time.

events.text: At a convocation of domains called to discuss, supposedly, something else, a god of the wind who carried your prayers has taken up with {b3_rival}'s messengers, and your prayers arrive late and slightly bent. Everyone is being scrupulously polite.

choices.text: Fetch the wind-god back with a bribe

ok.log: You find the wind-god at a cliff-top and offer it a better horizon, and your prayers arrive on time again.

fail.log: The wind-god takes the bribe and does the same as before.

effects.log: You ask {b3_rival}'s messengers to carry your prayers for a fee, and the awkward courtesy is the cheapest peace in a thousand years.
You accept the bent prayers and straighten them yourself, one by one, on the porch, and the faithful never notice.

events.text: When the prayers came in like weather, all from one side of the world, a young goddess of the Sea overtakes you both in the mortal prayers in a single season. You and {b3_rival} share a long, slow breath on the shared balcony. It is a very quiet kind of war.

choices.text: Share the balcony and the breath

effects.log: You and {b3_rival} breathe out together on the shared balcony, and one of you says the goddess is very good, and the other says she is.

choices.text: Offer the young goddess a seat on your side

ok.log: The young goddess, after a long look at the two of you, accepts a seat at your table, and {b3_rival} accepts one at hers.

fail.log: She refuses both seats with perfect courtesy.

choices.text: Pray to her, a little, for luck

effects.log: You pray to the young goddess, a little, for luck, and she is so astonished she gives it.

events.text: In a quiet corner of the Silent Hall, where no one is allowed to raise a voice, {b3_rival} sends a challenge by dream: "At the cross of the winds, at dawn." You wake with a sword in your hand and no memory of getting it. It will settle nothing and matter completely.

choices.text: Go to the cross of the winds at dawn

ok.log: You stand at the cross of the winds at dawn with your dream-sword, and the winds, bored, turn in your favour.

fail.log: The dawn is cold and the winds turn against you, and you go home bruised.

choices.text: Answer in a dream of your own

effects.log: You send a dream back, a short, polite one, in which you offer a different time and a good breakfast.

choices.text: Put the sword down and go back to sleep

effects.log: You put the sword under the pillow and sleep through the dawn, and {b3_rival} stands alone at the cross of the winds in a silly stance.

events.text: In the hour when mortals bring their offerings and the gods pretend not to count, a hymn in {b3_rival}'s temples calls you "the gentle one". It is sung with a tone that suggests the other word, the one that rhymes. It was done beautifully, and that is the insult.

choices.text: Sing the hymn back, with the rhyme

ok.log: You sing it through with the rhyme, cheerfully and in tune, and the temple of {b3_rival} has to stop its own choir laughing.

fail.log: You sing the rhyme a little flat, and the offering bowls fill for {b3_rival} that evening.

choices.text: Visit the temple and thank the choir

effects.log: You thank the choir in person, one by one, and the singers walk home with sore consciences and a better opinion of gentleness.

choices.text: Count the offerings, and be gentle

effects.log: You count what the hymn has brought your own altars since morning, and decide the word has done you no harm.

events.text: As the last of an age of worship burned down to its embers, a god of the Sky demands a tribute you cannot spare, and {b3_rival} sends it, quietly, with a note that says "A loan. Do not worry about the interest." It is the most irritating mercy you have ever received.

choices.text: Repay it within the season, with a bow

ok.log: The loan returns by the season's turn, in kind, and {b3_rival} accepts it as if it were a rare and difficult gift.

fail.log: The season turns before the tribute is ready, and the interest is quietly forgiven again.

choices.text: Send the interest anyway, as a joke

effects.log: You send a small bell as the interest, and a card marked 'to be rung when worried'. It rings in {b3_rival}'s temple all that year.

choices.text: Pay the Sky god and say little

effects.log: You pay the Sky god in full the next morning, and let the loan be a private thing between two old gods.

events.text: At the edge of the divine realm, where the clouds are thinner and the prayers are louder, {b3_rival} has founded a school for the daughters of the faithful on the next peak, and the peak has begun to rival your own. You send a more learned teacher. The faithful have taken sides.

choices.text: Send your best teacher and a gift

effects.log: You send the learned teacher, and a gift of books, and the faithful of both peaks decide to enjoy the competition.

ok.log: You sit at the back of a lesson and ask the one question the girls have been saving, and the teacher thanks you for it.

fail.log: You are recognised at the gate, and the lesson stops.

choices.text: Hold your own peak, and teach well

effects.log: You hold your peak and teach well, and in a hundred years the two peaks feed one another with students.

events.text: Between two harvests, in the lull when the faithful are too busy to pray, the Silent Hall's annual list of benefactors names {b3_rival} in the top row. Your name is below, in smaller script, spelled slightly wrong. It is hard to be angry at a very accurate lie.

effects.log: You take a pen to the list in the Silent Hall and fix your name, in the margin, once, in very small letters.

choices.text: Ask the clerk who ranks the rows

ok.log: The clerk, who ranks the rows by their own cryptic rule, admits it can be reviewed, and your name moves up a row.

fail.log: The clerk takes offence at the question, and your name moves down.

choices.text: Be hard to spell, and proud of it

effects.log: You decide to be a hard name to spell and, over three hundred years, make a hobby of the scribes' mistakes.

events.text: On the steps of the Will of Heaven, in full sight of everyone, the lamps of the Silent Hall go out in a sudden draught, and you and {b3_rival} are in the dark with a hundred gods and one match. The dispute will have to wait its turn.

effects.log: You hand {b3_rival} the match, and they strike it, and the hundred gods of the Silent Hall find their feet again.

ok.log: You strike the match in the draught, and it takes, and the hall remembers the sound.

fail.log: The match gutters out in the draught, and {b3_rival} has to light the next.

choices.text: Light the lamps in order of seniority

effects.log: You pass the flame from lamp to lamp in strict order of seniority, and by dawn the hall is lit and the dispute forgotten.

events.text: At the funeral of a minor god, to which both of you were obliged to go, you and {b3_rival} are the last two to leave a long, formal council. In the empty hall, {b3_rival} takes off their crown and rests it on their knee. The world below goes on being very large.

choices.text: Sit beside them on the dais step

effects.log: You sit on the dais step beside {b3_rival} and take off a crown of your own, and the hall, empty, hears nothing from two heads of state.

choices.text: Ask what they would do without it

ok.log: {b3_rival} tells you, with some surprise at telling, what they would do with an ordinary life, and you remember your own list.

fail.log: {b3_rival} puts the crown back on and says, lightly, it is late.

effects.log: You leave them the empty hall, and the lamps, and the length of the evening.

events.text: On the mountain where the gods go when they want to be alone together, Your favourite oracle has retired to a seaside villa on {b3_rival}'s coast, and writes to say she has taken up fishing and "other forms of faith". Loyalty among gods is a seasonal crop.

choices.text: Send her a net and good wishes

effects.log: You send the oracle a fine net and a note: 'Catch me something I did not foresee.' She sends back a fish and a vision.

choices.text: Visit her villa and consult her

ok.log: You consult the oracle on {b3_rival}'s coast, over a fish, and she tells you the one thing you were not asking, which is the right thing.

fail.log: She speaks in riddles, and the riddles are the fish's.

choices.text: Let her fish, and find another oracle

effects.log: You let her fish in peace and appoint an apprentice, and the apprentice is bad at it for a decade and then very good.

events.text: In a hall of the Throne of Storms, where arguments are held in thunder, the Throne of Storms offers {b3_rival} a seat on the Third Rank, and {b3_rival} asks for a fortnight to think, and spends it at your gate, saying nothing. The scales tip, as scales do.

choices.text: Open the gate and make them tea

effects.log: You open the gate and sit with {b3_rival} through the fortnight, saying nothing either, and the tea is the best you have ever shared.

choices.text: Tell them to take the Third Rank

ok.log: You tell {b3_rival} plainly to take the rank, and they look up as if you had handed them a key they thought lost.

fail.log: Your advice sounds like dismissal, and {b3_rival} leaves the gate unsure.

choices.text: Shut your door softly and let them think
