effects.log: You close your door softly and let them think, and the fortnight passes as a very quiet kind of company.

events.text: While a famine of belief moved across the lower lands, a race of the winds from the east edge to the west is proposed, with the Silent Hall as finish line and both of you as runners. Both of you know the rules and neither is following them.

choices.text: Run the east-west race flat out

ok.log: You cross the sky from east edge to west in a single breath and reach the Silent Hall as {b3_rival} is still ducking a cloud.

fail.log: You mistake a cloud for the Hall and are a league off course at the finish.

choices.text: Run it beside {b3_rival} and talk the whole way

effects.log: You run beside {b3_rival} the whole way, talking, and cross the line together, and the Silent Hall's judges disqualify the rule.
You offer to referee instead, and spend a pleasant afternoon at the finish with a whistle.

events.text: Under a sky you had both made, and could not quite agree on, {b3_rival} has commissioned a statue of the Will of Heaven with a faint, characteristic squint, and every worshipper knows the squint is yours. You have been a god long enough to know when a barb is a barb.

effects.log: You squint at the statue with great seriousness at its unveiling, until the worshippers laugh and the sculptor is quietly sent for.

ok.log: Your sculptor catches {b3_rival}'s habitual tilt so exactly that pilgrims bow to both statues in the same breath.

fail.log: Your sculptor makes {b3_rival} look rather wise, and the plan collapses.

effects.log: You let the squint stand. The sky you both made does not mind a squint, and the faithful come to prefer it.

events.text: In the court of the gods, in the slow part of the afternoon, {b3_rival} has spoken to the judge of the Silent Hall about your case. The judge will say only that it was "persuasive" and that {b3_rival} brought a pot of tea. Neither of you refers to it again.

choices.text: Bring tea to the judge yourself

effects.log: You bring the judge a better pot than {b3_rival} did, and the hearing is adjourned in a most civil tone.

choices.text: Ask the judge what was persuasive

ok.log: The judge says it was the brevity, and you cut your own pleadings by half from that day.

fail.log: The judge says that is a matter for the bench, and the bench is closed for the age.

effects.log: You accept the ruling without comment, and nobody in the Silent Hall is quite sure why you look so thoughtful.

events.text: At the turning of an age, in the court of the gods, the god of Fire challenges you both to light a lamp in the dark of the lowest sea. The first to reach the bottom keeps the privilege of naming it. You can hear the clouds thinking about it.

choices.text: Dive first, with a lamp in your teeth

ok.log: You reach the lowest dark first, lamp lit, and name it something absurd that the sea keeps.

fail.log: The dark outlasts your breath, and {b3_rival} carries the lamp the last of the way.

choices.text: Race {b3_rival} down, then name it together

effects.log: You tie your lines together at the bottom and name the place between you, and the god of Fire laughs and calls it a draw.

choices.text: Light your lamp at the surface

effects.log: You light your lamp at the surface and let it float down on its own, and a little lamp wins the privilege of being first.

events.text: At the feast of the twelve domains, three thousand years into the dispute, a child, praying at a spring, thanks {b3_rival} for the clean water. You made the spring. The child is five, and very sincere, and you cannot correct her. You compose three replies and send none.

choices.text: Let the child go on thanking {b3_rival}

effects.log: You let the child's thanks stand, and add a small blessing to the spring in your own name for later, when she is older.

choices.text: Visit as an old traveller and say so

ok.log: You appear as an old traveller and tell the child, without lying, who dug the spring, and she looks at you with great concentration.

fail.log: The child asks if you are a kind of cloud, and the lesson is lost.

choices.text: Drink from the spring and leave

effects.log: You drink from the spring, which is very good water, and go home quite content to be a rumour in it.

events.text: During a very long recess of the Book of Fates, a mortal king opens the gates of a city to the plague, and prays to both of you to hold it back. There is only room for one miracle. No other god is watching, which is a relief and a loss.

choices.text: Take the plague, and give {b3_rival} the king

effects.log: You divide the miracle: the plague yours, the king {b3_rival}'s, and the city lives.

choices.text: Hold the plague at the gate

ok.log: You stand in the gate of the city three nights, and the plague turns away from its door.

fail.log: The plague seeps through, and the gate wavers.

choices.text: Tell the king the truth about the gate

effects.log: You appear to the king in a dream and tell him the truth about the gate, and he closes it, late and stricken.

events.text: In the cold light of a star that neither of you had made, {b3_rival} comes to your shrine on a feast night and sits at the back with the pilgrims, in a plain cloak, and shares a loaf with a stranger. They go before you can speak. You do not mention it afterwards, either of you.

choices.text: Slide down the bench and share the bread

effects.log: You slide down the bench and take the end of the loaf from the stranger, and for one meal there are three pilgrims at the back.

ok.log: You catch {b3_rival} at the gate and say only 'come back', and they say they might, and the shrine hears both.

fail.log: You lose them in the crowd of the feast, and they are gone.

effects.log: You let them go unrecognised, which seems to be what they came for, and the feast goes on.

events.text: In the weeks after an unexpected miracle, whose credit was unclear, the scribes of the Silent Hall, who kept a good seat for you, have been moved to a different wing by a clerk who is a cousin of {b3_rival}'s. It is not theft. It is simply taking.

choices.text: Take your seat in the new wing

effects.log: You move to the new wing with your quill, and the clerks discover that a god at the next desk improves their handwriting.

ok.log: The cousin, startled by manners, admits the move was a favour, and the scribes are moved back with an apology.

fail.log: The cousin takes the question as an accusation, and the wing stays.

choices.text: Pack your scrolls and be easy

effects.log: You pack your scrolls and tell the scribes to follow their consciences, and a few of them do.

events.text: On the night the worshippers lit the great fires far below, {b3_rival} takes ill with a strange light-sickness and withdraws; the shrines go quiet, and the rivalry has no air. You catch yourself leaving offerings. It is a long time since anyone but them mattered this much.

effects.log: You leave offerings at {b3_rival}'s shuttered gate every dawn, from a little distance, and say they are for the shrine.

choices.text: Seek a cure for the light-sickness

ok.log: You find, in a closed scroll of the Silent Hall, a cure in three old ingredients, and {b3_rival} accepts it by silent messenger.

fail.log: The cure is a false lead, and the sickness stays.

choices.text: Mind your own shrines, and wait

effects.log: You mind your own shrines and wait, and are ashamed how little the temples please you without the rivalry.

events.text: In the Green Assembly's oldest grove, where the trees remember every oath, you and {b3_rival} are told to settle a boundary dispute by lot. The lot is drawn: it is a duel of echoes. Neither of you knows what that is. You feel very old, and very young.

choices.text: Fire the first echo into the canyon

ok.log: Your echo comes back as three, shaped like words, and {b3_rival} has no answer ready for the second.

fail.log: Your echo comes back as a laugh, and it is not yours.

choices.text: Ask the elders what an echo duel is

effects.log: You ask the elders, and learn that it means shouting your own name until it returns and wins, which is almost beautiful.

choices.text: Shout something kind into the valley

effects.log: You shout something kind into the valley and let the lot's loser be the valley itself.

events.text: In the Hall of Echoes, a young god asks {b3_rival} why you are so well-known. "Because they are punctual," says {b3_rival}, with great delicacy. You will remember this for a thousand years.

effects.log: You tell the young god that punctuality is a form of respect, and the young god leaves with a note to be on time to something.

choices.text: Ask {b3_rival} when they were last on time

ok.log: The Hall of Echoes repeats your question long enough that {b3_rival} has to answer it, and does so in good humour.

fail.log: The echo makes it sound like a complaint, and the young god chooses a side.

choices.text: Show up exactly on time, forever

effects.log: You make punctuality a small devotion, and in three hundred years it is the first thing mortals say about you.

events.text: At a convocation of domains called to discuss, supposedly, something else, Your oldest priest, near death, finds {b3_rival} by his bed, saying prayers for him in a voice no mortal should hear. The priest dies content. It changes nothing and everything.

effects.log: You enter and kneel on the other side, and the three of you share a long, still night that the priest does not wake from.

choices.text: Thank them, in a god's own voice

ok.log: You thank {b3_rival} in the old tongue, and the old man's face moves in his sleep like a man hearing a bell at home.

fail.log: The words come out too grand for a deathbed, and the room flinches.

choices.text: Withdraw, and leave them to it

effects.log: You withdraw before the last words, and leave {b3_rival} to the old man's hand as the one who did not need to be asked.

events.text: When the prayers came in like weather, all from one side of the world, a comet is due. {b3_rival} claims the right to be its patron by virtue of an old brief. You claim it by virtue of a newer one. The comet has no opinion. It is a small thing and the stakes are everything.

choices.text: Cite the newer brief, with the seal

ok.log: Your brief is the newer, the seal is true, and the comet takes your name in the sky like a nod.

fail.log: The seal is a century stale, and {b3_rival}'s old brief wins by a footnote.

effects.log: You offer to share patronage by hemispheres, and {b3_rival} agrees in a hurry, and the comet has one tail for each of you.
You stand under the comet and ask it, politely, who it prefers. It does not reply, and the matter is dropped.

events.text: In a quiet corner of the Silent Hall, where no one is allowed to raise a voice, {b3_rival} has been invited to open a new school of prayer, and in the opening address says: "I owe it all to the one who taught me patience." The audience applauds. The teacher is not named. Faith is a slow court.

choices.text: Attend the school as an unnamed guest

ok.log: You sit at the back of the school and are recognised by the hush of one old teacher, and your name is spoken in the second lecture.

fail.log: You sit at the back and are not noticed, and go home with a silence.

choices.text: Send {b3_rival} a cup, marked with your seal

effects.log: You send {b3_rival} a cup with your seal on the base, and a note that says only 'for the patience', and they stop mid-sentence at the next speech.

choices.text: Teach a quiet class of your own

effects.log: You teach a small class of your own and never mention the matter again, and the best students find their way to your door.

events.text: In the hour when mortals bring their offerings and the gods pretend not to count, a giant of the old order, awakened by quarrelling gods, rises from the plain. {b3_rival} is already at his ankle, speaking to him politely about the sea. Whatever happens, it will not be spoken of afterward.

choices.text: Speak to the giant about the mountain

effects.log: You speak of the mountain where he slept, and he sits, and gives a great sigh, and the plain remembers.

choices.text: Take the other ankle, and hold

roll.foeName: The giant of the old order

ok.log: You hold the giant's ankle against {b3_rival}'s, and for a heartbeat the old order thinks again.

fail.log: The giant shrugs, and you are a scattering of sparks across the plain.

effects.log: You get the plain's mortals out by the east road and leave the giant to a conversation about the sea.

events.text: As the last of an age of worship burned down to its embers, a moth lands on {b3_rival}'s hand at an evening gathering. They look at it for a long time and say, "It is probably nobody. But it is good to have visitors." You notice you are not angry.

choices.text: Offer them your lamp for visitors

effects.log: You lend {b3_rival} your lamp, and the moths of the gathering come to it from all over, and {b3_rival} counts them with a straight face.

choices.text: Ask what the moth might be

ok.log: You suggest the moth is the ghost of an old rival of both of you, and {b3_rival} laughs, and the moth stays on their hand.

fail.log: You suggest the moth is nobody, and {b3_rival} sighs, and the moth flies off.

choices.text: Watch the moth and say nothing

effects.log: You watch the moth with them in a long silence, and it is probably the nicest minute of the gathering.

events.text: At the edge of the divine realm, where the clouds are thinner and the prayers are louder, the farmers of the western valley, who once brought you the first sheaf, have taken to bringing it to {b3_rival}, who gives them a little more in return. You have your own habits to blame.

choices.text: Bring them the first sheaf yourself

effects.log: You carry the first sheaf up the western valley in your own arms, and the farmers' faces do something quite complicated.

choices.text: Offer a little more than {b3_rival} does

ok.log: Your offering of rain in the dry week outbids {b3_rival}'s extra grain, and the farmers return, with a sheaf.

fail.log: Your rain arrives a day late, and {b3_rival}'s extra grain is already eaten.

choices.text: Take what the farmers choose to give

effects.log: You take the sheaf, when it comes, and not before, and the valley's loyalty grows back slowly, like barley.

events.text: Between two harvests, in the lull when the faithful are too busy to pray, you are given a domain you did not ask for, the Quiet, and {b3_rival} sends a hand-lettered banner: "Congratulations. It suits you. Please do not use it on me." The ladder only goes one way, and every god is on it.

choices.text: Hang the banner in your hall

effects.log: You hang the banner in the main hall of the Quiet, and {b3_rival} comes by to see it, and is startled to find it framed.

choices.text: Use the Quiet on them, once, lightly

ok.log: You lay a hush on {b3_rival} for an hour, lightly, and they enjoy it more than they will say.

fail.log: The hush goes slightly wrong and silences the whole feast.

effects.log: You settle into the Quiet like a coat that was always yours, and your first act is to stop doing things.

events.text: On the steps of the Will of Heaven, in full sight of everyone, the Throne of Storms has ordered a thunder-fight between the two of you over the plains, to dry a flooded valley. The valley is not impressed. The court is quieter than usual.

choices.text: Meet the thunder with your own

ok.log: Your thunder meets {b3_rival}'s over the plain, and the flooded valley dries in the din, to the mortals' surprise.

fail.log: Your thunder cracks and {b3_rival}'s rolls over it, and the valley stays wet.

choices.text: Fight with the thunder pointed away

effects.log: You and {b3_rival} fight the thunder-fight a mile apart, with the claps pointed at the sea, and the valley drains on its own.

choices.text: Tell the Throne it will dry by itself

effects.log: You send word to the Throne that the valley will dry in a week, and it does, and nobody thanks you.

events.text: At the funeral of a minor god, to which both of you were obliged to go, {b3_rival} remarks at a council of the Green Assembly that your rains are "reliable", the way one calls a mule reliable. The Assembly murmurs that this is high praise. All the gods are looking at you to see how you take it.

choices.text: Call a downpour, and call it a mule

ok.log: Your rains arrive on a mule's schedule over the Assembly's own roof, and nobody calls the mule anything else.

fail.log: The rain misses, and the Assembly sighs about reliability.

choices.text: Accept the praise as it was offered

effects.log: You thank {b3_rival} for the highest praise a god gives a mule, and the Assembly applauds the word in an awkward rush.

choices.text: Go and water the funeral garden

effects.log: You say nothing and go out to the funeral garden and water it, reliably, until the ceremony is over.

events.text: On the mountain where the gods go when they want to be alone together, a bridge your faithful built is washed out; the next morning it is rebuilt, rope and plank, with a prayer carved in the post: "for the other side". You owe them now, and both of you know it.

choices.text: Carve a prayer on the other post

effects.log: You carve your own prayer on the far post, in plain letters, and the bridge is blessed from both ends.

choices.text: Cross it with the faithful, at dawn

ok.log: You cross at the head of your own pilgrims, and the new rope holds all the way over, to the cheers of the other bank.

fail.log: A plank gives, mildly, mid-span, and the faithful are fished out of the shallows.

choices.text: Leave the bridge as it was found

effects.log: You leave it as it stands, rope and plank and one extra prayer, and the faithful use it without remarking on the change.

events.text: In a hall of the Throne of Storms, where arguments are held in thunder, the Green Assembly proposes a contest of orchards: three years each, one tree, judged by the old goat at the grove's gate. The other gods are watching with a kind of bored interest.

choices.text: Graft your tree from three old stocks

ok.log: The graft takes, the tree fruits in a single summer, and the old goat at the grove's gate bleats once, in favour.

fail.log: The graft rots, and the goat eats the fruit anyway.

choices.text: Swap seedlings with {b3_rival} at the start

effects.log: You swap seedlings, and the contest becomes a matter of who tends the other's tree better, to the goat's confusion.

choices.text: Plant it and go away for three years

effects.log: You plant the tree, go away for three years, and come back to a tree that has been quietly doing its own work.

events.text: While a famine of belief moved across the lower lands, a hymn the Green Assembly sings every spring, whose last verse you wrote, now credits {b3_rival} in the margin of the hymnal. The record is dry, which is the worst of it.

choices.text: Add your name to the hymnal in ink

effects.log: You add your name to the margin of the hymnal in careful ink, beside {b3_rival}'s, and the verse becomes a joint work.

choices.text: Sing the last verse as written

ok.log: You sing the last verse in the Assembly, and the Assembly, as one body, remembers who wrote it.

fail.log: You sing the verse a half-tone sharp, and the Assembly looks at the margin.

effects.log: You leave the margin as it is, and sing the verse as you wrote it every spring without a footnote.

events.text: Under a sky you had both made, and could not quite agree on, a river of the dead has overflowed into the river of the living; the two gods who share a bank are asked to keep the mortals from drinking. You are, for one night, simply on the same side.

choices.text: Dam the river of the dead

ok.log: You dam the river of the dead with a hill of your own, and {b3_rival} holds the living bank.

fail.log: The dam leaks, and the dead water laps at the living.

choices.text: Put a sign on the shared bank

effects.log: You put up a sign on the shared bank in your own hand, 'Do not drink', and {b3_rival} adds one in theirs. Both are read.

choices.text: Sit with the mortals at the shore

effects.log: You sit with the mortals at the water's edge and keep their hands from the cup, till morning.

events.text: In the court of the gods, in the slow part of the afternoon, {b3_rival} asks you whether you still dream, and when you say you do, they say, with great care, "Of what?" It is the most honest hour of your acquaintance.

choices.text: Tell them the dream, as it is

ok.log: You tell them the dream in the plain words you used to use, and {b3_rival} listens without once trying to improve it.

fail.log: The dream comes out as a boast, and {b3_rival} nods politely and does not ask again.

effects.log: You ask them the same, and the answer is a small and surprising thing, and neither of you says anything for a while.

choices.text: Say you do, and leave it there

effects.log: You say only 'Yes', and the word does for both of you.

events.text: At the turning of an age, in the court of the gods, a holy mountain on your border has begun to glow faintly in {b3_rival}'s colour. Nobody has asked the mountain. You feel the ground move, if there were ground.

choices.text: Ask the mountain what it wants

ok.log: The mountain, after a century of thought, says that it prefers to be asked, and glows in two colours at once, to be fair.

fail.log: The mountain says nothing at all, and glows on.

choices.text: Hold a festival on your side of it

effects.log: You hold a festival on your slope with lanterns in your own colour, and the mountain, being shy, shows a little blue at the rim.

choices.text: Let the mountain keep its glow

effects.log: You let the mountain choose its own colour, and the pilgrims go up it without caring who is lit.

events.text: At the feast of the twelve domains, three thousand years into the dispute, a new god of Fortune is crowned in the Heavenly Court, and neither you nor {b3_rival} is invited to the coronation, and both of you go anyway, uninvited, as guests of the gate. Whatever the court says, the two of you know.

choices.text: Go uninvited, and stand at the gate

effects.log: You and {b3_rival} stand at the gate of the coronation together, uninvited, and the gatekeepers, being gods, let you both through.

choices.text: Toast the new god from the back

ok.log: You toast the new god of Fortune from the back, and fortune, for once, answers the toast with a small coin from nowhere.

fail.log: Your toast is drowned out by a trumpet, and nobody sees it.

choices.text: Watch from the gate and go home

effects.log: You watch from the gate and go home, and consider the new god's chances, which are better than yours were.

events.text: During a very long recess of the Book of Fates, {b3_rival} arrives with a sword-bearing angel for a second, a nervous cousin, and a flask of mortal wine, and says, "I have decided to enjoy this." Someone is already laying odds, and you will not look.

choices.text: Meet the party with a duel of your own

ok.log: You bring a nervous cousin of your own, and a better cook, and win the duel at the third course.

fail.log: The cooking is too good, and you lose the duel at the second course.

effects.log: You decide, in the end, to enjoy it with them, and the duel is a long afternoon of dinner and small blows.

choices.text: Pour the wine and decline the bout

effects.log: You pour the wine for the second and the angel, take the day off from dueling, and raise a cup of tea to a draw.

events.text: In the cold light of a star that neither of you had made, a pilgrim returns from {b3_rival}'s mountain with a charm that says, in tiny letters, that you should be forgiven for existing. It sells very well. The court is not sure whether to laugh.

choices.text: Buy one, and wear it to court

effects.log: You wear the charm on your sleeve at the next audience, and the whole court discovers how much it would like to be forgiven too.

ok.log: Your own second line, in smaller letters, reads 'and be remembered', and the charm sells out twice as fast.

fail.log: Your second line reads as a grudge, and pilgrims drop it in the river.

choices.text: Forgive the pilgrim, and say so

effects.log: You forgive the pilgrim for the purchase, with a small blessing, and let the charm do what it was sold to do.

events.text: In the weeks after an unexpected miracle, whose credit was unclear, the wind-god, who owes you a favour, delivers it to {b3_rival} by mistake, and {b3_rival} brings it to you, wrapped in cloth, and says only, "It was addressed to you." Gods have long memories, and this one will be kept.

choices.text: Thank the wind-god for the error

effects.log: You send the wind-god a kite and a note of thanks for its excellent mistake, and the wind-god blushes the whole of a week.

ok.log: The cloth falls away on a favour so small and so exact that {b3_rival} actually laughs.

fail.log: The favour turns out to be a debt of yours, and {b3_rival} returns it with a look.

choices.text: Put the favour to use quietly

effects.log: You spend the favour on a harvest you had given up for lost, and say nothing at all of its route.

events.text: On the night the worshippers lit the great fires far below, {b3_rival} stakes a claim to the high pass between your valleys. You stake a claim to the lower. The middle is left for the mortals, who build a shrine to nobody. You would rather win than be right.

choices.text: Walk the middle shrine and bless it

effects.log: You bless the mortals' shrine to nobody, and nobody, in gratitude, begins to answer to your name.

choices.text: Argue the lower pass at the Assembly

ok.log: You argue it so reasonably that the Assembly writes the lower pass into your domain in the margin.

fail.log: You argue it so heatedly that the Assembly sends you home to cool.

choices.text: Surrender the lower pass for the middle

effects.log: You let {b3_rival} have the high and the low and keep the middle for the mortals, and the mortals, in time, remember.

events.text: In the Green Assembly's oldest grove, where the trees remember every oath, a statue of a god pulling a child from a flood stands in the great square of the mortals. The face is {b3_rival}'s, though the arms, you notice, are yours. You have the facts, and they have the room.

choices.text: Stand beside the statue, arms up

effects.log: You stand beside the statue with your arms in the same posture and wait for the crowd to notice, which it does.

choices.text: Commission a plaque for the arms

ok.log: Your plaque reads 'The arms are also a god's', and the crowd, delighted, rubs them for luck.

fail.log: The plaque is lost in the sculptors' guild.

choices.text: Let the child in the flood be the point

effects.log: You let the statue be about the child in the flood, who is real, and who lives to a great old age.

events.text: A few centuries after the last time you had both said "never again", the Green Assembly's oldest tree is struck by a bolt, and its sap runs black; {b3_rival} hacks at the branch and says, "Hold the trunk." There will be no one to witness, and so it will matter.

ok.log: You hold the trunk through the long night of the tree's black sap, and {b3_rival} cuts the branch that was dying.

fail.log: The trunk sways, and the sap runs on your hands.

effects.log: You tell {b3_rival} which branch is truly dead, by the ring of its sap, and they swing.
You fetch the gardeners and the oldest axe, and the Assembly saves the grove, with some quarrel as to whose idea it was.

events.text: At a convocation of domains called to discuss, supposedly, something else, {b3_rival} sends a gift to the temple of a god long dead: a single white lamp, lit. They leave no name. You know the hand that did it. For a moment the dispute is only an old habit.

choices.text: Light a second lamp beside it

effects.log: You place a second white lamp beside {b3_rival}'s on the dead god's step, and the two burn at the same height all night.

ok.log: You find, in the Silent Hall's oldest ledger, the god's real name and domain, and your lamp acquires a purpose.

fail.log: The ledger is missing, and the god stays a shadow.

choices.text: Know the hand, and say nothing

effects.log: You know the hand and say nothing, and the lamp burns by itself in the dusk of the old god's temple.

events.text: When the prayers came in like weather, all from one side of the world, a young hero, who prayed to you since a child, has been offered a sword by {b3_rival} on the eve of his first battle, and has accepted it. Everyone is being scrupulously polite.

choices.text: Meet the hero on the eve of battle

effects.log: You meet the young hero at the camp-fire and tell him what the sword cannot do, and give him the one thing it cannot give him.

choices.text: Send a blessing to ride beside the sword

ok.log: Your blessing rides in his scabbard through the first battle, and the sword and the prayer turn out to be a good team.

fail.log: Your blessing goes astray in the fighting, and the hero swears at the sky.

choices.text: Wish him well and stay out of it

effects.log: You wish him well, in a short prayer, and stay out of a battle he asked another god to share.

events.text: In a quiet corner of the Silent Hall, where no one is allowed to raise a voice, a thousand-year vow ends for {b3_rival}, and they return from the mountain, changed and taller, with a hymn nobody can place. The court is silent for it. It is a very quiet kind of war.

choices.text: Ask them to sing the hymn

effects.log: You ask {b3_rival} to sing the hymn, and they do, to the empty hall, and your hands feel a little cold.

choices.text: Learn the hymn from the silence

ok.log: You listen for three nights outside the hall until you can hum it, and the court wonders how you know.

fail.log: You learn only the rhythm, and the court hears a drumbeat.

effects.log: You let the court be silent, and are silent with it, as the hymn goes out over the lower lands like weather.

events.text: In the hour when mortals bring their offerings and the gods pretend not to count, a cloud-bridge is built for a duel at the top of the world. The loser must carry the winner's prayers for a hundred years. The crowd is vast, and silent. It will settle nothing and matter completely.

choices.text: Cross the bridge and fight at the summit

ok.log: You win the summit by a step, and {b3_rival} carries your prayers for a hundred years with a faint, comic sigh.

fail.log: You lose the summit by a step, and carry {b3_rival}'s prayers for a century, grumbling.

choices.text: Offer to carry each other's prayers

effects.log: You offer a swap on the bridge at the summit, and the silent crowd melts into something like applause.

choices.text: Stay below and bless the bridge

effects.log: You stay below and bless the bridge, which is the only decent thing that has happened to it, and the crowd goes home.

events.text: As the last of an age of worship burned down to its embers, the Throne of Storms' herald announces the year's weather and, in a whisper, adds that {b3_rival} predicted yours would be dull. It was not. It was merely adequate. It was done beautifully, and that is the insult.

choices.text: Make the next year's weather memorable

ok.log: Your weather breaks in a rare gold storm that the mortals call a marvel for centuries, and the herald corrects the record.

fail.log: The weather is merely adequate again, and the herald repeats the prophecy.

choices.text: Ask the herald for the prediction in writing

effects.log: The herald hands over the scroll, and you pin it to your temple door under a small, courteous heading: Adequate.

choices.text: Let the embers go out in peace

effects.log: You let the age end with its dull weather, and the mortals warm themselves at it without a thought for the forecast.

events.text: In the Hall of Fates, a clerk lets drop that your name has been quietly moved up on the list of those due a blessing. The clerk was asked to by {b3_rival}. It is the most irritating mercy you have ever received.

choices.text: Move a name on the list for them

effects.log: You find a name of {b3_rival}'s own on a lower list, and move it, silently, one rung, and let the clerks believe it a clerical error.

ok.log: The clerk, charmed, lets drop a second favour {b3_rival} did you, and your list of debts is complete for the first time.

fail.log: The clerk panics and burns the list, and your name is back where it was.

choices.text: Accept the blessing in good order

effects.log: You accept the blessing when it arrives and say a short and honest thank-you to whoever was involved.

events.text: Between two harvests, in the lull when the faithful are too busy to pray, the Silent Hall has made it a matter of record: if a prayer from the plains is answered by both of you in the same hour, the later answer is void. The faithful have taken sides.

choices.text: Answer the plains prayer a breath earlier

ok.log: Your answer lands an instant before {b3_rival}'s, and the later one dissolves with a faint sigh of the Silent Hall.

fail.log: Your answer lands an instant after, and is void by the letter of the rule.

effects.log: You propose alternate hours, and the plains, which have been praying both ways, learn to call you by turns.
You leave the plains' prayers to {b3_rival} that season and pick up the neglected hill ones, which turn out to be warmer.

events.text: At the festival of the first harvest, {b3_rival} is carried through the streets on a litter of grain. The grain was yours, and so was the festival. It is hard to be angry at a very accurate lie.

choices.text: Carry the other end of the litter

effects.log: You take the rear pole of the litter, quietly, and the procession carries both of you through the streets, one in glory, one in sweat.

choices.text: Open your granaries to the festival

ok.log: Your open granaries make the festival twice as plentiful, and the town cheers a god it can see.

fail.log: Your granaries are found half empty, and the town doesn't cheer.

choices.text: Eat the grain, and enjoy the festival

effects.log: You eat your portion of the grain with the rest, and the festival is as good a festival as any.

events.text: At the funeral of a minor god, to which both of you were obliged to go, a volcano under a holy island begins to wake. {b3_rival} pleads with its fire, and you with its mountain, and neither of you can say who the volcano is listening to. The dispute will have to wait its turn.

choices.text: Plead with the mountain, as agreed

effects.log: You plead with the mountain while {b3_rival} pleads with the fire, and the island holds its breath.

choices.text: Stand between the island and the fire

ok.log: You stand at the island's lip and take the heat on your shoulders, and the fire, impressed, sinks.

fail.log: The heat takes you as it takes anything, and the island is evacuated.

choices.text: Move the pilgrims off the island first

effects.log: You move the pilgrims to the mainland, one boat after another, and the volcano wakes to an empty shrine.

events.text: On the mountain where the gods go when they want to be alone together, you overhear {b3_rival} in the sky-gardens telling a young god the story of your quarrel, honestly, and with surprising fairness to you. The world below goes on being very large.

effects.log: You thank {b3_rival} afterwards for being fair, and they say it was merely accurate, and walk off very straight.

choices.text: Join the telling, and correct a detail

ok.log: You step into the garden and correct a detail in your own disfavour, and the young god's mouth falls open at the pair of you.

fail.log: You step in too soon, and the young god falls silent.

choices.text: Stay behind the hedge, and listen

effects.log: You stay behind the hedge and hear the rest, and the rest is fair too.

events.text: In a hall of the Throne of Storms, where arguments are held in thunder, Your steward of ten ages tells you, with great embarrassment, that {b3_rival} has asked him to organise their feast days. He would like your blessing. Loyalty among gods is a seasonal crop.

choices.text: Ask him to organise both feast days

ok.log: You ask him to run both calendars, and he looks so stunned that the two temples stop pretending he is a prize.

fail.log: He hears the offer as pity and walks out.

choices.text: Give your blessing, and a few tips

effects.log: You give your blessing and three tips about {b3_rival}'s temper at feasts, and he writes them down and cries a little.

choices.text: Thank him for ten ages, and let go

effects.log: You thank him for ten ages of unbroken service and release him with a handshake, which an ordinary god does not often receive.

events.text: While a famine of belief moved across the lower lands, you are made the arbiter of a dispute between two pantheons, and {b3_rival} is made your second. Neither of you understands the order of the honours. The scales tip, as scales do.

choices.text: Name {b3_rival} as your equal in the ruling

effects.log: You write {b3_rival} into the ruling as co-arbiter, and the two pantheons, outraged and soothed, settle in a week.

ok.log: You decide in an afternoon, with a sentence on each side, and the pantheons accept it out of surprise.

fail.log: Your decision satisfies nobody, and the pantheons appeal.

choices.text: Take the honours and share the paperwork

effects.log: You take the honours and share the paperwork, and the order of precedence is forgotten by the next age.

events.text: Under a sky you had both made, and could not quite agree on, {b3_rival} declines to duel, citing a vow, and instead proposes a contest of patience: whichever blinks first at the dawn of the solstice shall pay a debt. Both of you know the rules and neither is following them.

choices.text: Hold your eyes open at the solstice dawn

ok.log: You keep your eyes open through the solstice sunrise, and {b3_rival} blinks at the very edge of the light.

fail.log: You blink at the first ray, and the debt is yours to pay.

effects.log: You blink at the same instant, on purpose, and {b3_rival} laughs, and the debt is cancelled by a very old smile.
You sleep through the dawn and leave the debt to the next age, and wake up well rested.

events.text: At the shrine you share with {b3_rival} on the border, you find the offering bowl on your side deeper by a hair than {b3_rival}'s, and polished. You have been a god long enough to know when a barb is a barb.

choices.text: Fill the other bowl with your own

effects.log: You pour your offering into {b3_rival}'s bowl at midnight. It overflows by morning, and the border shrine is the talk of two valleys.

ok.log: {b3_rival} comes at dawn to find their bowl brighter than yours, and says nothing, and brings a cloth.

fail.log: The bowl turns out to be an heirloom, and polishing it is taken as an insult.

choices.text: Accept the depth and the polish

effects.log: You accept both. A bowl is a bowl, and the pilgrims at your side of the border are plainly the happier for it.

events.text: At the turning of an age, in the court of the gods, {b3_rival} has quietly rewritten the closing line of your hymn to remove the awkward rhyme, and the hymn is much improved. Nobody will say how. Neither of you refers to it again.

choices.text: Read the new line at the next feast

effects.log: You sing the new closing line at the next feast with feeling, and {b3_rival} in the third row studies the ceiling.

choices.text: Match it by mending one of theirs

ok.log: You find the one clumsy line in a hymn of {b3_rival}'s and mend it, and the two hymns sound the better for each other.

fail.log: You mend the wrong line, and {b3_rival}'s choir wonders aloud who did it.

choices.text: Let the hymn go on improving

effects.log: You say nothing of the rewrite, and the faithful simply find the hymn sweeter than they used to.

events.text: At the feast of the twelve domains, three thousand years into the dispute, a temple clock of the old kind has been installed in a lowland village, and both of you have been asked to declare it sacred. The clock is wrong by an hour. You can hear the clouds thinking about it.

effects.log: You declare the clock sacred and wrong by exactly an hour, and the village sets its life by the difference.

choices.text: Fix the clock yourself, by night

ok.log: You fix it by night and it is right by morning, and {b3_rival} stands before it with nothing to declare.

fail.log: You loosen a spring, and the clock gains an hour more.

choices.text: Let {b3_rival} declare it, and be gracious

effects.log: You let {b3_rival} declare the clock sacred, and the village, wrong by an hour, is all the happier for being told it is blessed.

events.text: During a very long recess of the Book of Fates, {b3_rival} has taken credit, in a council of the Throne of Storms, for a thunderclap that was nothing of theirs. The thunder god laughs and does not contradict. You compose three replies and send none.

choices.text: Ask the thunder god to contradict it

ok.log: The thunder god, put on the spot, laughs once and says the clap was a poor thing, and was not {b3_rival}'s.

fail.log: The thunder god laughs and says everyone's thunder sounds alike.

choices.text: Make a thunderclap of your own

effects.log: You make a clap of your own over the Throne of Storms, a good one, and it is nobody's but yours.
You pocket the three replies for a more useful day and go home with a sense of having been very dignified.

events.text: In the cold light of a star that neither of you had made, a great number of the Heavenly Court's scrolls go up in flame, and {b3_rival} hauls out the oldest, and hands it to you through the smoke. No other god is watching, which is a relief and a loss.

choices.text: Take the oldest scroll and run

effects.log: You take the scroll in both hands and carry it out through the smoke, and the Heavenly Court is a little less empty.

choices.text: Go back in for the Book's index

ok.log: You come out with the index, singed at the edge, and the court's records have a spine again.

fail.log: You come out with nothing but a singed sleeve.

choices.text: Open the windows and clear the smoke

effects.log: You break the windows of the long gallery, and the smoke goes out, and the scrolls that were left are saved.

events.text: On the shortest day of the year, {b3_rival} comes to your gate with a bundle of wood and says, "I thought you might be cold." You are not. You say thank you. You do not mention it afterwards, either of you.

effects.log: You light the fire together on your hearth, and they stay long enough to be offered tea, which they accept with a very small bow.

choices.text: Send them home with a coat

ok.log: Your coat fits them oddly and well, and they wear it to the next council, and nobody dares comment.

fail.log: The coat does not fit, and they wear it anyway out of politeness.

choices.text: Say thank you, and stack the wood

effects.log: You say thank you and stack the wood by the door, and burn it slowly over a season.

events.text: On the night the worshippers lit the great fires far below, a small god of the crossroads, whom you had befriended, is spotted dining with {b3_rival} at a house of the Throne of Storms, and waves. It is not theft. It is simply taking.

choices.text: Join the table and order something

effects.log: You sit down at the table and order the house dish, and the crossroads god, delighted, introduces everyone.

ok.log: You wave back in the middle of a crowded road, and half the house of the Throne decides you are the easy one to like.

fail.log: You wave back and trip on a cloud, and the house laughs at you kindly.

choices.text: Remember that friends are not property

effects.log: You remember that a small god's friendships are not yours to hold, and take the long way home.

events.text: In the Green Assembly's oldest grove, where the trees remember every oath, {b3_rival} loses a following in a rebellion of the faithful. They come to you, hat in hand, and ask only for a night's lodging. It is a long time since anyone but them mattered this much.

choices.text: Give them the best room, no questions

effects.log: You give {b3_rival} the best guest room and ask no questions, and in the morning they have left the bed made, which is a god's way of weeping.

choices.text: Offer to help win the following back

ok.log: You walk the villages with {b3_rival} in the dust, and the faithful, seeing the two of you, forgive more than they planned to.

fail.log: The villagers close their doors on both of you.

effects.log: You lodge them for a night and say nothing, and the night does the work of a hundred speeches.

events.text: A few centuries after the last time you had both said "never again", a pair of mortal children, playing at gods, stage a mock-duel in your name and {b3_rival}'s in the dust of a village square. Both of you watch, and take notes. You feel very old, and very young.

choices.text: Join the children and take a side

effects.log: You kneel in the dust beside the children and take a side, and {b3_rival} takes the other, and the village sees two gods lose to a ten-year-old.

choices.text: Judge their duel with a straight face

ok.log: You judge the mock-duel with a straight face, and award the prize to the smallest child, and {b3_rival} applauds from across the square.

fail.log: Your face breaks first, and the children are offended.

effects.log: You watch and take your notes, as does {b3_rival}, and neither of you says what you learned.

events.text: At a convocation of domains called to discuss, supposedly, something else, {b3_rival} has been telling the minor gods of the sea-coast that you once took three centuries to answer a prayer. It was two. They are counting. You will remember this for a thousand years.

choices.text: Correct the count before the coast

effects.log: You write the real date in the temple register, in clear letters, for the minor gods of the sea-coast to see.

choices.text: Answer a prayer within the hour, twice

ok.log: The coast counts your two answers in one hour and crosses out the three centuries with a flourish.

fail.log: One of the answers goes to the wrong prayer, and they count that too.

effects.log: You let the sea-coast gods count, and in a century they have so much to count about the others that you slip down the page.

events.text: When the prayers came in like weather, all from one side of the world, a storm that was meant for your coast breaks over {b3_rival}'s instead. They stand under it with their arms folded, as though it were a joke between friends. It changes nothing and everything.

choices.text: Go and stand under it with them

effects.log: You go to {b3_rival}'s coast and stand beside them under the storm, arms folded, and say it was meant for you after all.

choices.text: Call the storm off, if it will listen

ok.log: The storm, impressed by your tone, goes out to sea, and {b3_rival} says it was no great weather anyhow.

fail.log: The storm takes your temper as an invitation and breaks over both of you.

choices.text: Send dry cloaks to their shore

effects.log: You send a hundred dry cloaks to their coast and say nothing of the hundred and first, which is for them.

events.text: In a quiet corner of the Silent Hall, where no one is allowed to raise a voice, {b3_rival} proposes a game of riddles at the Equinox feast, each loser to give up a blessing for a year. You accept before you have read the terms. It is a small thing and the stakes are everything.

choices.text: Play the riddle game for the stake

ok.log: You win, by the closest margin the Silent Hall has seen, and {b3_rival} hands over a year of their blessing with a straight face.

fail.log: You lose to a riddle about salt, and your blessing is theirs for a year.

choices.text: Rewrite the terms before the first riddle

effects.log: You read the terms aloud and discover the loophole in clause three, and the two of you amend them with a pen.
You play to lose, gracefully, and the Equinox feast learns a very good riddle.

events.text: In the hour when mortals bring their offerings and the gods pretend not to count, a mortal historian writes that the god who first taught the people to make bread was {b3_rival}. You taught them. The historian was asleep at the time. Faith is a slow court.

choices.text: Wake the historian with a loaf

ok.log: You leave a loaf at the historian's elbow with a note that shows the date, and the book is revised in the next edition.

fail.log: The loaf is eaten by the historian's cat, and the note goes with it.

effects.log: You invite {b3_rival} to a baking, and they turn out to be hopeless, and the mortal watchers see the bread's real inventor.

choices.text: Let the people eat, and not read

effects.log: You let the people eat the bread and leave the history to others, as bread is better than the history of bread.

events.text: In the dream-hours, a mortal is trapped in a nightmare that has two gods' names in it. {b3_rival} takes the left door. You take the right. Whatever happens, it will not be spoken of afterward.

choices.text: Open the right door and go in

ok.log: You open the right door, say the sleeper's real name, and the nightmare unbuckles itself.

fail.log: The right door opens onto a second door, and you are late.

choices.text: Call across to {b3_rival} through the wall

effects.log: You call across to {b3_rival} through the wall of the dream, and the two of you speak once and truly, in the sleeper's voice.
You sit at the sleeper's bedside and keep the lamp, and the mortal wakes with the dawn.

events.text: At the edge of the divine realm, where the clouds are thinner and the prayers are louder, you find that {b3_rival} has been keeping a small garden of the plants you named on your first day of godhood. It is weedy, and loved. You notice you are not angry.

choices.text: Pull the weeds out beside them

effects.log: You and {b3_rival} pull weeds side by side until dusk, and the first-day plants straighten like old soldiers.

ok.log: You name the plants in the order you named them, and {b3_rival} writes each on a slate, and the garden is thereby a school.

fail.log: You mix up two of the names, and {b3_rival} corrects you without malice.

choices.text: Walk through, and don't step on anything

effects.log: You walk through the garden very carefully, stepping on nothing, and leave it exactly as loved as it was.

events.text: Between two harvests, in the lull when the faithful are too busy to pray, a great number of the pilgrims at your solstice festival wear a small badge in {b3_rival}'s colour, and are clearly delighted by the fact. You have your own habits to blame.

choices.text: Wear a badge in your own colour

effects.log: You wear a badge in {b3_rival}'s colour at your own solstice, with a straight face, and the pilgrims laugh so hard they come back next year.

choices.text: Hand out your badges at the gate

ok.log: Your badges at the gate are gone by noon, and the pilgrims wear both and are delighted.

fail.log: Your badges are a fraction too gaudy, and are left in the porch.

choices.text: Let the pilgrims wear what they like

effects.log: You let the pilgrims wear what they like, and the solstice goes on, the better for variety.

events.text: On the steps of the Will of Heaven, in full sight of everyone, the Heavenly Court announces a new category of honour for "distinguished perseverance in the face of one particular rival". You are both on the list. The ladder only goes one way, and every god is on it.

choices.text: Accept the honour with {b3_rival}, on stage

ok.log: You and {b3_rival} receive the honour together on the dais, bow in the same breath, and the Heavenly Court laughs and cannot stop.

fail.log: You bow a moment late, and the court's laughter is only half kind.

effects.log: You propose renaming it for a rival worthy of the name, and {b3_rival} seconds, and the amendment is carried.
You ask to be removed from the list with thanks, and the Court enters a note that you have persevered even in this.

events.text: At the funeral of a minor god, to which both of you were obliged to go, {b3_rival} sends you a letter of challenge that is plainly a love-letter to a god of the Sea, misaddressed. They have asked you to forward it and do not mention the challenge again. The court is quieter than usual.

choices.text: Forward it with a witty note

effects.log: You forward the letter to the god of the Sea with a note: 'Mistaken for a challenge. Please be gentle.' They reply within the hour.

choices.text: Read the letter first, and learn something

ok.log: You read it, which you should not have, and learn the one thing about {b3_rival} that makes the quarrel look small.

fail.log: You read it, and it is too private, and you stop at the second line.

choices.text: Seal it and send it on, unread

effects.log: You seal the letter and send it on unread, and {b3_rival}'s gratitude, when it comes, is formal and total.

events.text: On the mountain where the gods go when they want to be alone together, a choir of the Will of Heaven is rehearsing a new anthem. {b3_rival}, listening, says that the soloist is "nearly as good as" you, and the soloist is crushed. All the gods are looking at you to see how you take it.

ok.log: You take the soloist's part for a single verse, softly, and the choir finishes the anthem in a hush.

fail.log: Your verse is flat, and the soloist forgives you out of pity.

choices.text: Tell the soloist they are better

effects.log: You tell the soloist they are the better by a clear measure, and {b3_rival} blinks at the sound of a compliment going the other way.
You applaud with the rest and go down the mountain humming it, which does more for the soloist than a debate would.

events.text: In a hall of the Throne of Storms, where arguments are held in thunder, you find a handful of seeds in your temple porch, all labelled in {b3_rival}'s spiky hand with the names of the plants that grow in your valley and not theirs. You owe them now, and both of you know it.

choices.text: Plant the seeds in your temple porch

ok.log: The seeds sprout in your porch before the season turns, and the valley smells of {b3_rival}'s weeds for years.

fail.log: The seeds do not take, and the porch stays bare.

choices.text: Send back a packet of your own

effects.log: You send a packet of valley seeds to {b3_rival}'s mountain, each labelled in your own better hand, and neither of you mentions the exchange.

choices.text: Label the porch, and leave it

effects.log: You hang a small label by the seeds that says only 'from the neighbours', and leave the rest to the weather.

events.text: While a famine of belief moved across the lower lands, a rival hymn to {b3_rival} has gone round your valley, the tune catchier than yours. You commission a better tune. They commission a better poet. The other gods are watching with a kind of bored interest.

ok.log: Your tune is carried over three valleys by the weekend, and {b3_rival}'s poet admits it, to the poet's credit.

fail.log: Your tune is too grand to hum, and the valley hums {b3_rival}'s.

choices.text: Learn {b3_rival}'s hymn and sing it well

effects.log: You learn {b3_rival}'s hymn and sing it in your own temple, perfectly, and the valley has to decide who owns the tune.

choices.text: Let the valley hum what it likes

effects.log: You let the valley hum what it likes, and it hums both, and the faithful are not the poorer for it.

events.text: Under a sky you had both made, and could not quite agree on, you find your own wise saying in a book of proverbs, attributed to "the old god of the north", whom you know to be {b3_rival}. The record is dry, which is the worst of it.

choices.text: Write the saying down with its date

effects.log: You write the saying down again, with its date, in a book of your own, and leave it where the north god will find it.

choices.text: Ask the north god to explain

ok.log: {b3_rival} admits, with some grace, that the saying was borrowed, and puts your name beside it in the next printing.

fail.log: {b3_rival} insists it is a common saying, and the page stays.

choices.text: Use the proverb at their expense

effects.log: You use the proverb in an audience, with its true attribution, and the room does the rest.

events.text: In the court of the gods, in the slow part of the afternoon, a comet, thrown off course, strikes a distant shore, and the tide it makes will drown a thousand villages. {b3_rival} shouts the plan across the clouds. You are, for one night, simply on the same side.

choices.text: Shout the plan back across the clouds

effects.log: You shout back the plan's flaw and its fix, and {b3_rival} amends it in the air, and the tide goes east.

choices.text: Turn the tide with your own domain

ok.log: You push the tide aside with everything you have, and the thousand villages are only wet.

fail.log: The tide is bigger than you, and your push is a bad guess.

choices.text: Warn the villages, and run the roads

effects.log: You run the coast roads in the shape of a fox, waking every village, and the villages are empty when the water comes.

events.text: At the funeral of an old god, {b3_rival} stands beside you and hums, under their breath, a slow tune you used to hum. They stop when they notice. It is the most honest hour of your acquaintance.

effects.log: You take up the tune where they stopped, and they find the note again, and the old god's funeral has, for a minute, music.

ok.log: {b3_rival} says they learned it from you, in a year neither of you will name, and you both stand a while longer.

fail.log: {b3_rival} says they cannot remember, and the tune is gone.

effects.log: You let them hum alone, which is clearly what the tune wanted, and the funeral goes on.

events.text: At the feast of the twelve domains, three thousand years into the dispute, a mortal queen who used to send you the first fruits has started sending them elsewhere, with a courteous letter explaining that {b3_rival} sends better weather. You feel the ground move, if there were ground.

choices.text: Write to the queen about the weather

ok.log: Your letter lays out three summers of weather, honest and plain, and the queen, struck, sends the first fruits back.

fail.log: Your letter sounds like a complaint, and she keeps her fruits where they are.

effects.log: You send the queen a fine summer without comment, and the first fruits come back unasked.
You accept the queen's letter and her decision, and send her your blessing for her harvests wherever they go.

events.text: During a very long recess of the Book of Fates, you make a grand error in an audience of the Will of Heaven, and the whole hall waits for {b3_rival} to pounce. They stand, and say it was theirs. Whatever the court says, the two of you know.

choices.text: Stand up and say it was yours

effects.log: You stand and say that the error was yours, in full, and {b3_rival} sits down looking slightly cheated of a favour.

choices.text: Thank them in private, with a gift

ok.log: You thank {b3_rival} privately with a gift of the one scroll they have wanted, and they accept it as if it were a small snub.

fail.log: The gift is misread as a bribe, and the thanks are cooler.

choices.text: Let the hall believe what it likes

effects.log: You let the Will of Heaven believe whoever it wishes to believe, and the hall dissolves back into its audience.

events.text: In the cold light of a star that neither of you had made, a harvest feud over a field spills into a mortal brawl, and the two of you, called to arbitrate, end up on opposite sides, shouting from the clouds. Someone is already laying odds, and you will not look.

choices.text: Shout your side from the clouds

ok.log: Your voice carries the length of the field, and the mortals, stunned, stop brawling and take your side.

fail.log: Your voice cracks on the clouds, and the brawl grows louder.

choices.text: Cross the clouds and arbitrate together

effects.log: You cross the clouds to {b3_rival}'s side and arbitrate together, shouting the same verdict in two voices, and the brawl blushes.

choices.text: Settle the field by splitting the crop

effects.log: You divide the field by the crop, and the brawl dissolves in a puzzled argument about arithmetic.

events.text: In the weeks after an unexpected miracle, whose credit was unclear, {b3_rival} sends a basket of dried flowers on your day of founding, arranged into a pattern that, seen from above, spells a word that is not quite insulting. The court is not sure whether to laugh.

effects.log: You read the pattern out at dinner, flower by flower, and the not-quite-insult turns out to be a rather good pun on your name.

ok.log: Your pressed leaves spell a longer word, a much kinder one, and the gods who see it wonder who started this.

fail.log: Your leaves wilt in transit and spell nothing at all.

choices.text: Put the basket on a shelf

effects.log: You put the flowers where the light is good and let them speak for themselves for the rest of the age.

events.text: On the night the worshippers lit the great fires far below, a mortal prays that two gods remember each other kindly, and the answer arrives on {b3_rival}'s side of the border as a tray of honey cakes. Gods have long memories, and this one will be kept.

choices.text: Share the cakes with the border mortals

effects.log: You carry the tray to the border villages and divide it, and the mortals who prayed for kindness eat their answer with sticky fingers.

choices.text: Send the tray back, with an extra

ok.log: Your tray goes back with a jar of your own honey on it, and {b3_rival} keeps the jar and sends the tray again.

fail.log: Your tray arrives crumbs, and {b3_rival} returns the jar sealed.

choices.text: Eat one, and say thank you

effects.log: You eat a single cake on the border, standing, and decide the mortal's prayer was well answered.

events.text: In the Green Assembly's oldest grove, where the trees remember every oath, the god of the Mountains has declared that the next to move a stone from the summit to the foot, by faith alone, shall hold the pass. {b3_rival} brings a donkey. You would rather win than be right.

choices.text: Move the stone by faith alone

ok.log: The stone shifts by itself the last few paces, as if surprised at the fuss, and the pass is yours.

fail.log: The stone stays where it is, in peace, and {b3_rival}'s donkey sets off down the hill.

effects.log: You walk down beside the donkey and talk to it, and the god of the Mountains declares the pass held by both sides and the animal.

choices.text: Sit on the stone and watch

effects.log: You sit on the stone and watch the donkey go by, and the god of the Mountains finds the whole matter increasingly funny.

events.text: A few centuries after the last time you had both said "never again", a priestess praises {b3_rival} in a public hymn for the well that you dug. She has never met you, and says so kindly. You have the facts, and they have the room.

choices.text: Visit the priestess and drink at the well

effects.log: You drink at the well with the priestess and say nothing of the dig, and she tells you the well-water is blessed by {b3_rival}.

choices.text: Leave a sign by the well

ok.log: Your sign, a small stone with a carving of a spade, is read by the priestess a year later, and she writes a second hymn.

fail.log: The sign is taken for a boundary marker and moved.

effects.log: You dig another well in another valley, unsigned, for the pleasure of having done it.

events.text: At a convocation of domains called to discuss, supposedly, something else, the wall of the world, which holds the sea in its bed, gives a small crack in the night, and only two gods of the Throne are near enough to hear it. There will be no one to witness, and so it will matter.

choices.text: Report the crack to the Throne at once

effects.log: You send the crack's exact position to the Throne at a run, and the Throne, shaken from a nap, sends help.

choices.text: Hold the crack closed with your hands

ok.log: You hold the crack with your open hands until the Throne's masons come, and the sea does not move.

fail.log: The crack widens under you, and you are drenched to the bone.

choices.text: Sit beside the crack with {b3_rival} and wait

effects.log: You and {b3_rival} sit beside the crack until dawn and say very little, and the wall holds as if ashamed.

events.text: When the prayers came in like weather, all from one side of the world, {b3_rival} asks, in the middle of a long, dull ceremony, whether you ever think of the day you were nobody. You say you do. They say, "So do I." For a moment the dispute is only an old habit.

choices.text: Tell them about the day, in full

effects.log: You tell {b3_rival} about the day you were nobody, in detail, with the cold, and they tell you theirs, and the ceremony runs on without you.

choices.text: Ask what they would tell that nobody

ok.log: {b3_rival} says they would tell that nobody to be kind to the next one, and you both nod at the wall.

fail.log: {b3_rival} shrugs and says nobody was no use to anyone, and turns away.

choices.text: Say yes, and attend to the liturgy

effects.log: You say yes, and attend to the liturgy, and the ceremony, being long, is gentle enough to be forgiven.

events.text: In a quiet corner of the Silent Hall, where no one is allowed to raise a voice, {b3_rival} has set up an inn on the pilgrim road to your shrine, serving excellent soup. The soup is turning your pilgrims into {b3_rival}'s. Everyone is being scrupulously polite.

choices.text: Taste the soup, and ask for the recipe

effects.log: You taste the soup, nod, and ask the cook for the recipe, and {b3_rival}'s inn becomes a temple of mutual flattery.

choices.text: Open an inn of your own, down the road

ok.log: Your inn opens with a stew nobody forgets, and the pilgrims go between the two with an extra stomach.

fail.log: Your stew is thin and the pilgrims stick with the soup.

choices.text: Eat well and keep your shrine open

effects.log: You eat well at the inn, keep your shrine open, and let the pilgrims see that a god can be hungry too.

events.text: In the hour when mortals bring their offerings and the gods pretend not to count, a god of the east, whom you had both taught, rises to the rank of Warden and, at the ceremony, bows low to the two of you in one gesture. It is a very quiet kind of war.

choices.text: Bow back in the same gesture

effects.log: You bow back to the Warden in the same gesture, and {b3_rival} does too, and the three of you look like a very old diagram.

choices.text: Make a speech about the Warden

ok.log: You say three true things about the Warden's youth, and {b3_rival} adds a fourth, and the Warden has the look of a lamp lit from both sides.

fail.log: Your speech is a little long, and {b3_rival} adds only a cough.

effects.log: You let the Warden be proud, and keep your rival's elbow in sight, in the interest of the evening.

events.text: As the last of an age of worship burned down to its embers, the Green Assembly proclaims a dance-duel at the spring festival, and the loser must wear a crown of nettles for a month. {b3_rival} has been practising. It will settle nothing and matter completely.

choices.text: Dance the spring dance at full tilt

ok.log: You dance with such unstudied delight that the Assembly stands, and {b3_rival}'s rehearsed steps are lovely and second.

fail.log: You step on your own hem and take the nettle crown.

choices.text: Teach {b3_rival} your own steps, at midnight

effects.log: You teach {b3_rival} your steps in the dark, and they teach you theirs, and the spring dance becomes a joint pageant.

choices.text: Sit it out, and weave a crown

effects.log: You sit it out and weave a crown of nettles with gloves on, and give it to whoever loses, as a tribute.

events.text: Ten years on, the sparrows of your valley have taught their young the cadence, and the cadence has crossed to the next valley, where it is a harvest song. Farmers hum your name over the sheaves without knowing it. {b3_rival} hears it from a hill and does not smile.

effects.log: You send a thanks on the wind. A single sparrow returns with a feather in its beak, which is the reply.

choices.text: Teach the birds a second tune

effects.log: You teach the sparrows a second tune, a rude one about {b3_rival}. It is a hit in the barn.
You let the farmers hum. A name in a song is worth more than a name on a plaque.

events.text: Ten years on, the eastern valley's shrine has grown into a small temple, and the roof that {b3_rival} patched is the one the pilgrims touch for luck. The patch is clumsy, in a hand that is not a builder's, and has become the most beloved thing in the valley.

effects.log: You tell {b3_rival} about the pilgrims. They go red to the ears, and send a bag of nails.
You leave the patch alone, and put up a small sign: "Mended with care by someone who would not say."

choices.text: Build them a shrine of their own

effects.log: You build {b3_rival} a small shrine in the valley, a wayside one. They do not mention it. They visit.

events.text: Ten years on, the bridge-city is a metropolis, and its people still argue about who blessed it. A statue in the square shows two gods back to back, each holding the same arch. The city's motto is "Neither, and both."

effects.log: You visit the square with {b3_rival}, in disguise, and listen to the argument. It is vigorous, kind, and wholly unscientific.
You settle the question in a dream, to the city's mayor. Half the city believes it. Half do not.
You join the argument at a tavern table, in character, and win by a sheer volume. {b3_rival} buys the next pot of tea.

events.text: Ten years on, the temple "to the god who stilled the river" is being enlarged, and the builders ask who the god is, so that they might carve a face. The abbot, with some shame, sends for you and {b3_rival} to settle it. The inscription is in the abbot's hands.

choices.text: Tell the abbot it was you

effects.log: You tell the abbot it was you. He nods, and chisels a line beneath the inscription, and the face is yours, with {b3_rival}'s eyebrows.
You say it was both, which is untrue and also fair. The face is a blend, and rather strange, and beloved.
You say it was a river that chose to be still. The abbot weeps and carves a river. It is the best thing in the temple.

events.text: Ten years on, the city that screamed into both of you is rebuilt in the shape of a pair of hands, joined: the north half in the style of {b3_rival}'s temples, the south in yours. Pilgrims cross the central bridge to pray to both.

effects.log: You cross the bridge with {b3_rival}, in plain cloaks, unrecognised. In the middle there is a small, damp shrine to the two of you, and it is the best thing in the city.

choices.text: Leave an offering on each half

effects.log: You leave an offering on each half, one for the north, one for the south. Both are taken.

choices.text: Ask the mayor how it works

effects.log: You ask the mayor how the city manages two gods. "Badly, with a great deal of tea," she says.

events.text: Ten years on, the altar of the dead god is a small, well-kept shrine, and its candles have not gone out in all that time. {b3_rival} still comes, in a plain cloak, to replace them. You have started to come by on the same evening, as if by chance.

effects.log: You replace a candle together in silence. When the flame takes, {b3_rival} says, "He would have liked that."

choices.text: Bring a candle of your own

effects.log: You bring a candle of your own. It burns a different colour, and {b3_rival} says it suits the altar.

choices.text: Ask who the dead god was

effects.log: You ask who the dead god was. The answer is long, strange, and surprisingly funny.

events.text: Ten years on, the old priest of your oldest shrine dies at {b3_rival}'s temple, and in his will asks to be buried at yours. {b3_rival} brings the coffin to your gate with their own hands, and bows, formally, and says, "He wanted to come home."

effects.log: You bury him with honours, and {b3_rival} stands at the back of the funeral. It is a good funeral.
You thank {b3_rival}, and they say it was nothing, and look as if it were everything.
You ask what changed his mind. "You did," says {b3_rival}. "He said so on his deathbed. I had nothing to do with it."

events.text: Ten years on, the domain of Mist has become its own small kingdom of grey meadows and soft rains, and {b3_rival} sends an invitation to its opening ceremony: a plain card, with a single line. "I should like it if you came. You were the first to say it could exist."

effects.log: You attend with a gift, a pot of fern, and {b3_rival} cries openly into a handkerchief at the moment of the first fog.

choices.text: Send an apology for the doubt

effects.log: You send an apology for ever doubting. The reply is a mist, drifting through your window, with a smell of rain.

choices.text: Ask to be allowed to rule a corner

effects.log: You ask for a small corner of the Mist. {b3_rival} gives you a hill, and the hill is grey, and you grow fond of it.

events.text: Ten years on, the farmers of the rain-contest have grown fond of the two of you, and every year they hold a small festival at which a pair of paper clouds is thrown into a pond. The rain falls on whichever cloud floats longer. This year, it is yours.

effects.log: You dance at the festival with {b3_rival}, badly, to a fiddle. The farmers cheer.
You let the clouds float on, side by side. The rain, that year, is gentle.
You challenge {b3_rival} to a real contest of rains, as a gift to the farmers. It rains for nine days, and they remember it all their lives.

events.text: Ten years on, the poet who was told about the snail has published a verse, in which a snail and a god have a long argument about patience. The god wins. {b3_rival} buys forty copies for the Hall and writes in the margin: "Hear, hear."

effects.log: You write the poet a letter of thanks, and he answers with another verse, shorter and better.
You send a leaf to the snail, via a messenger, and the snail eats it. That is the reply.

choices.text: Read the margin note aloud at the next feast

effects.log: You read the margin note aloud at the next feast, with feeling. {b3_rival} claims it was ironic and nobody believes them.

events.text: Ten years on, the god of Famine returns to your border, older and gentler, and sits down to a meal at your table. "I was told not to come here," he says, "by a friend of yours." He does not say which. You know.

effects.log: You feed him well, and the old god weeps into his rice. Famine is a lonely trade.
You ask what {b3_rival} told him. "That you were worth a lot of trouble," says the god, "and that they would do it again."
You offer him a post in your granary, as a counter-clerk of shortage. He takes it, with a kind of stunned gratitude.

events.text: Ten years on, the mortal queen has a successor, who sends a polite summons: please attend the anniversary of the soup. You and {b3_rival} are both seated, by the same herald, at the head of a long table. The soup, this year, is rather good.

effects.log: You pass the salt to {b3_rival}. It begins a polite chain that runs the entire length of the table.

choices.text: Propose a toast to the queen

effects.log: You propose a toast to the late queen, and {b3_rival} seconds it, and the room is moved.

choices.text: Ask the new queen what she wants

effects.log: You ask the new queen what she wants of the gods. Her answer is so honest and so simple that both of you are quiet for the rest of the meal.

events.text: Ten years on, the miracle-play in which {b3_rival} plays your part is performed again, but this year the actor wears a mask with your face, and the audience cheers. The troupe has moved on from a joke to something nearer to truth.

effects.log: You go and see the play, hidden at the back. The actor has your walk. Your whole body goes hot.
You send the actor a gift, a rare drum. The troupe plays it for the next ten years.
You tell {b3_rival} you saw the play. They say, "I did not do the walk," and look very guilty.

events.text: Ten years on, the sleeping harvest god wakes briefly, as he does once a century, and looks about with a face like a dropped loaf. He says to you, with great warmth, "I dreamed of two voices, singing." {b3_rival} stands behind you, pale.

choices.text: Tell him it was a dream

effects.log: You tell him it was a dream. He nods, a little sadly, and goes back to sleep. The land stills.
You sing the lullaby, and {b3_rival} joins, off-key, and the old god smiles in his sleep.
You ask what he heard. He yawns: "Harmony." You and {b3_rival} look at each other, appalled.

events.text: Ten years on, the field {b3_rival} used to own is still worked, and the farmer who has it writes to the gods, politely, asking whom to thank for the good soil. {b3_rival} stares at the letter and asks if you would like to help them write the reply.

effects.log: You help write the reply, and the farmer is thanked by two gods in one hand. He frames it.
You tell the farmer the soil was the previous owner's. He weeps, and plants a row in their name.
You let {b3_rival} write alone, and read the reply later. It is two lines long and is the best thing you have ever seen them write.

events.text: Ten years on, the bard who sang of {b3_rival} returns, a little older, and sings a new ballad about the two of you, in which each of you is the villain of the other's story. It is brilliant. Both of you attend, in different cloaks, and weep at different verses.

effects.log: You pay the bard handsomely, and he leaves with a full purse of faith and a note about writing a third ballad.

choices.text: Ask him to sing it for {b3_rival}

effects.log: You ask the bard to sing it for {b3_rival}, in the Hall. The Hall is silent for a full minute afterwards.

choices.text: Argue with a line in it

effects.log: You argue with a line in it, afterwards, over tea. The bard changes it, and the ballad improves.

events.text: Ten years on, the footnote in the Book of Fates beside {b3_rival}'s name is now a full page, in which the Hall records the effect of their rise on the realm. You are mentioned in the margin, twice, as "the necessary opposition", and the Hall means it as praise.

effects.log: You read the page with {b3_rival}, aloud. They are mortified. Then they laugh. Then they cry.

choices.text: Write a margin of your own

effects.log: You write a margin of your own, thanking {b3_rival} for being worth opposing. The Hall allows it.

choices.text: Ask to be struck from the page

effects.log: You ask to be struck from the page, as unseemly. The Hall refuses with delicate firmness.

events.text: Ten years on, the arm-wrestling has become a tournament in the cloud-bank, with a trophy keg and a cheering crowd of minor gods. You and {b3_rival} are the last two in the final, and the table is cracking. The judge, a tiny goddess of grain, is in tears.

effects.log: You go all out. The table shatters, the keg goes flying, and both of you land in the flour. {b3_rival} wins by a hair, laughing.

choices.text: Propose a draw, and give the keg to the crowd

effects.log: You propose a draw, and the keg goes to the crowd, who are delighted.
You let {b3_rival} win, with the dignity of someone who has chosen to. They know. They say nothing, and they are grateful.

events.text: Ten years on, the statue with your squint stands in a hundred shrines, and children play at squinting at each other. The Will of Heaven grows tired of it and asks you and {b3_rival} to put a stop to the squinting, with a polite official letter.
