choices.text: Squint back at the Will of Heaven

effects.log: You squint back, formally, in the hall. The Will of Heaven is not amused, and then it is.

choices.text: Ask {b3_rival} to make a new statue

effects.log: You ask {b3_rival} to make a new statue. They accept as though it were a commission from a king. The new one has a straighter nose.
You stop the children yourself with a small thunderclap. They squint harder at the sky.

events.text: Ten years on, the judge of the Silent Hall retires, and in a quiet farewell tells you that {b3_rival} came to see her once a year after your case, always with tea, and never asked for anything. "I think they wanted me to know you were worth defending," she says.

choices.text: Visit {b3_rival} with a pot of tea

effects.log: You visit with a pot of tea. {b3_rival} is mortified, and delighted, and puts the kettle on.
You send a brief note of thanks. The reply is one line: "It was not for thanks."

choices.text: Save the judge's tea-set for them

effects.log: You ask for the judge's old tea-set, and send it to {b3_rival} as a gift. It is the best thing you ever gave.

events.text: Ten years on, the lamp at the bottom of the sea burns steadily, and the sea-gods have made it a feast day. It has no name. The god of Fire visits yearly to check it is not out. {b3_rival} dives with you, as they did the first time, and sits beside the light.

effects.log: You name the lamp together, in the language of the sea. The word has no equivalent above the waves.
You agree to tend the lamp in turn, a year each. The sea has never been kept so well.
You leave it nameless, and the lamp burns, and the old fire-god nods approval from afar.

events.text: Ten years on, the child who thanked the wrong god for the spring is a woman of fifteen, and now thanks both of you, with exactness, each in their turn. She has drawn a diagram of the water's path and where each of you touched it.

effects.log: You praise the diagram, to the young woman's face, and she goes pink. {b3_rival} adds their own praise from a different cloud.

choices.text: Ask her to teach other children

effects.log: You ask her to teach other children the way of the water. She does, and the school she founds grows.

choices.text: Correct one detail in her diagram

effects.log: You correct one detail in her diagram, gently. She is delighted to be corrected by a god.

events.text: Ten years on, the plague-king is dead, and his city rebuilt, and the people tell the story that two gods fought the plague with a single miracle between them. The version they tell gets bigger each year. In it you and {b3_rival} are twins.

effects.log: You correct the story to a pilgrim, who looks horrified and then thrilled, and tells it again with the correction in.
You embrace the story, and let the pilgrims call you twin gods. {b3_rival} accepts, shyly, after a decade of hesitation.

choices.text: Send the mortals a better miracle

effects.log: You send the mortals a better miracle, a clean spring on the old plague ground. They do not guess whose it is.

events.text: Ten years on, the stranger who shared a loaf with {b3_rival} at the festival has become a regular at your shrine, and sits at the back, and says nothing. Once, finally, he whispers to you: "A friend of mine was a god once. I wondered what they were like."

effects.log: You tell him about {b3_rival}: the tea, the bad jokes, the plain cloak. He listens as if to scripture.
You share a loaf with him in silence. It is a good loaf.

choices.text: Ask him who his friend was

effects.log: You ask him. He smiles and does not answer, and he is gone before you can ask again.

events.text: Ten years on, the scribes who were moved have been moved back, with an apology, and a new rule in the Silent Hall: seat allocations must be signed by both of the gods concerned. {b3_rival} signs yours and you sign theirs, in the same hand.

effects.log: You sign for them kindly, with a small flourish, and the clerk nearly weeps at the paperwork.

choices.text: Move the scribes to a better wing

effects.log: You move the scribes to a better wing, with windows. {b3_rival} offers them lunch.
You let the rule be. It is the best bureaucracy you ever suffered.

events.text: Ten years on, {b3_rival} recovers from the light-sickness, and wakes in your guest-room, where you had them brought. They look at the ceiling, and at you, and at the tea beside the bed. "You kept the shrines running," they say, hoarsely. "I know. I heard."

effects.log: You say it was nothing. {b3_rival} smiles, tiredly. "You are a terrible liar," they say.
You ask what they heard. "Your prayers," says {b3_rival}. "You prayed for me. I did not think you knew how."
You hand them the tea. They drink it, and sleep, and in the morning they are well.

events.text: Ten years on, the duel of echoes, which nobody understood, has been decoded by a young scholar: a duel in which two gods speak to each other from opposite mountains, and the one whose voice returns clearer wins. The Hall asks for an official match.

effects.log: You shout first, and your voice returns, tinged with gold. {b3_rival} shouts and theirs returns whole. A draw.
You whisper, and the echo carries it perfectly. {b3_rival} hears every word, and says nothing, and does not move.
You suggest a duet. The echoes make a chord, and the Hall declares it a new art form.

events.text: Ten years on, the sellers of the charm that forgives you for existing have gone into business with the temple of {b3_rival}, and the two of you are named in the same small print. A pilgrim brings you one as a gift, without irony.

effects.log: You wear the charm on a cord. It makes you smile in unlikely moments, which is its purpose.
You send {b3_rival} a charm of your own, with a different line: "Forgiven for the same." They keep it on their desk.
You shut the stall down by decree. The charms sell for twice as much, as relics.

events.text: Ten years on, the wind-god's favour comes due again, and this time arrives at the right address, but with a note from {b3_rival} pinned to it: "It was mine to deliver. I held it for a decade. I am sorry."

effects.log: You return the favour to {b3_rival}, the old one. They are so surprised that they hold the wind-god's hand for a long, long moment.

choices.text: Use the favour on a mortal

effects.log: You use the favour on a mortal village. The wind turns in their harvest, and the name on the prayer is both yours.
You reply to the note: "No harm done." It is a comfortable lie, and truer than most.

events.text: Ten years on, the middle of the high pass is a shrine to nobody, and nobody's shrine is the busiest in the realm. Pilgrims bring offerings, pray to no name, and leave in good spirits. The god of the Mountains is bemused. {b3_rival} comes to see it.

effects.log: You and {b3_rival} stand at the shrine to nobody, in plain cloaks, and give an offering together. It feels like something.

choices.text: Claim it for the two of you jointly

effects.log: You propose that the shrine be dedicated to both. The pilgrims object. It stays nameless.

choices.text: Ask the priestess what she prays for

effects.log: You ask the priestess what she prays for. "That they would stop fighting and have a cup of tea," she says. Neither of you can look at her.

events.text: Ten years on, the statue in the square, with {b3_rival}'s face and your arms, has begun to crack at the neck. The mortals fear for it. A mason offers to repair it with a plaque listing both gods. The city council debates the plaque for a decade.

effects.log: You pay for the repairs yourself, with a miracle of plaster, and tell the council to put what plaque they like.
You ask {b3_rival} to share the cost. They send three times as much. The mason is overwhelmed.
You let the neck crack. It makes the statue look as if it is thinking, and the city finds that profound.

events.text: Ten years on, the great oak of the Green Assembly, black-sapped, has healed into a strange, dark-barked tree, and the leaves are the colour of copper. The Assembly names it for you and {b3_rival}, and holds a spring ceremony under it each year.

effects.log: You attend with {b3_rival}, and sit under the tree. The copper leaves fall on your hair. Neither of you brushes them off.

choices.text: Plant a seed from the tree

effects.log: You plant a seed from the tree on your own hill. It takes root and is the pride of your grove.
You refuse the naming, with a modest speech. The Assembly names the tree for the two of you anyway.

events.text: Ten years on, the lamp {b3_rival} left at the dead god's temple has never gone out. The priests are baffled and grateful. You go to check, one evening, and find a small card beside it: "Not for anyone. Just for the light."

choices.text: Add a card of your own

effects.log: You add a card of your own: "Seen." The lamp, for a moment, seems to burn brighter.
You tell {b3_rival} you found the lamp. They stare at the floor and say "It was not meant to be found."
You tend the lamp quietly, in the dark hours, for the rest of the age.

events.text: Ten years on, the young hero who took {b3_rival}'s sword is an old general and has retired, and returns the sword to the god with a note: "It served me better than I deserved." {b3_rival} comes to your temple, awkwardly, with the sword in a cloth.

effects.log: You accept the sword, for the shrine's wall, and hang it between your two crests. It looks right there.
You tell {b3_rival} to keep it, and they put it on a nail in their kitchen, where it hangs, thrilled.

choices.text: Ask what the hero said of you

effects.log: You ask what the hero said of you. "He said you were stricter," says {b3_rival}, "and he preferred it."

events.text: Ten years on, {b3_rival} returns from the mountain after a thousand-year vow, and the hymn they bring is a lullaby for gods, a thing nobody had thought to write. The court sings it for a year, and then the mortals, and it comes back as a plain folk song.

effects.log: You hum the lullaby at dusk, in your shrine. A moth lands on your sleeve.

choices.text: Tell {b3_rival} it is the best hymn of the age

effects.log: You tell {b3_rival} it is the best hymn of the age. They say nothing at all, and then, "I wrote it for you."
You write a counter-melody. The two together make a canon, and it is performed at the next solstice.

events.text: Ten years on, the cloud-bridge duel, never held, is remembered as the greatest contest that never happened. The crowd that gathered went home, and then came back, and then built an annual fair on the spot. Stalls sell paper swords. Children duel in the street.

effects.log: You buy a paper sword from a child, and fight {b3_rival} on the bridge, in front of the fair, and lose, hilariously.
You ask for the fair's proceeds. They go to a school.
You stay away, and watch from a cloud, and discover you prefer it.

events.text: Ten years on, the story of your three centuries has become a proverb among the sea-gods: "slow as a prayer on the third tide." The minor gods say it to each other, fondly. {b3_rival} has stopped telling the story, and, awkwardly, looks sorry.

effects.log: You tell the true story, kindly. It was two centuries. The sea-gods laugh and amend the proverb to "two."

choices.text: Answer a prayer at once, to prove a point

effects.log: You answer a prayer within the hour, as a show. The proverb survives that too, and grows a footnote.
You let the proverb stand. Every culture needs a slow one, and you do it with style.

events.text: Ten years on, the coast where the storm meant for you struck {b3_rival} is the best fishing in the realm. The fishermen call the storm "the Kind One", and pray to both of you at the harvest. {b3_rival} still scowls at the praise, and the scowl is not entirely real.

choices.text: Offer {b3_rival} a share of the catch

effects.log: You send {b3_rival} a share of the catch in a basket woven by the fishermen. They send back half the basket.
You visit the coast together, in plain cloaks, and eat fried fish on the quay. Nobody guesses.

choices.text: Make the storm an annual feast

effects.log: You make the storm an annual feast, with {b3_rival}'s name on the first dish. They pretend to be furious.

events.text: Ten years on, the riddles have become a sport of the Equinox feast, and the stakes are blessings, and the champions are your two oldest temples. {b3_rival} proposes a final round, between the two of you, and the answer is a word you are both afraid to say.

effects.log: You say the word first. It is "stay." {b3_rival} says it second, and the hall goes silent.

choices.text: Pass, and honour the other's turn

effects.log: You pass, and {b3_rival} answers. It is the right word. You raise your cup.
You ask for a new riddle. {b3_rival} produces one in a heartbeat. It is a good one, and you do not know the answer.

events.text: Ten years on, the historian who credited {b3_rival} with the bread has been corrected by a younger scholar, who discovered an old kitchen-god tablet. The old scholar is in despair. {b3_rival} writes to him to say that the error was a "gift", and that the truth was better.

effects.log: You write to the old scholar, too, to say he was not wrong to be confused. He writes back a very long, grateful letter.

choices.text: Send the young scholar a thank-you

effects.log: You send the young scholar a note and a small blessing. She does not know from whom, and is sure it is a coincidence.
You let the record stand corrected. The bread, as the old kitchen-god well knows, tastes the same.

events.text: Ten years on, the mortal you saved from the nightmare is an old man, dying, and in his last dream the two gods who held the doors appear again, kindly, one on each side of his bed. {b3_rival} is there. They look up, startled, as you arrive.

effects.log: You sit down beside {b3_rival}, and the two of you hold the old man's hands until he is gone. Neither of you speaks of it after.
You sing him the old lullaby, and {b3_rival} joins, and he dies smiling.
You leave them to it, and wait outside the door. It is a long time before {b3_rival} comes out.

events.text: Ten years on, the garden of your named plants is a landmark, and {b3_rival} has added a gate, a bench, and a small sign: "Please do not tell them it is mine." Visitors walk through in awed silence, and a few, quite by accident, weed.

choices.text: Add a plant of your own

effects.log: You add a plant, a hardy and unlovely one. {b3_rival} writes its name on the sign.
You bring the bench a cushion, red. It is stolen within the week.

choices.text: Sit in the garden with them

effects.log: You sit in the garden with {b3_rival} one evening, saying nothing. A moth lands on the bench between you.

events.text: Ten years on, the pilgrims in {b3_rival}'s colours have taken to staying at your inns, since the soup there is better, and singing your hymns at your table. The two congregations have blurred. A priest of yours is married to a priest of theirs.

effects.log: You perform the blessing at the wedding. {b3_rival} stands on the other side, and gives the cup to the bride.
You hold a joint feast on the border, and the colours mingle. A vast, noisy picnic ensues.
You ask {b3_rival} to stop the mixing, and they look at you as if you had asked them to stop the tide.

events.text: Ten years on, the new honour for "distinguished perseverance in the face of one particular rival" is given to you and {b3_rival} at a ceremony of the Heavenly Court. You must both give an acceptance speech. Neither of you has written one.

effects.log: You speak first, and the speech is good: short, wry, true. {b3_rival} follows with a better one. The court weeps.
You let {b3_rival} speak first. They stand silent for a full minute, then sit down. It is the most eloquent speech of the age.
You propose a joint speech, extempore, a line each. It goes terribly well, and nobody can say why.

events.text: Ten years on, the misaddressed love-letter turns out to have been to a god of the Sea who did, after all, reply. The two have been exchanging letters ever since. {b3_rival} blushes when you mention it, and confesses that they owe you for the postage.

effects.log: You offer to carry the letters yourself. {b3_rival} accepts, with a hundred reservations.
You tease them kindly. {b3_rival} throws a cushion, and misses, and it is the first time you have seen them laugh at themselves.
You wish them well, and mean it. The letter you carry to the Sea is lighter than any prayer you have borne.

events.text: Ten years on, the dried flowers have been pressed into a book, and the book into a shelf, and the shelf is now in the Hall of Fates, where no one knows what it is. {b3_rival} comes by to look at it, and says, bleakly, "I did not think it would last."

choices.text: Tell them what the pattern said

effects.log: You tell them the pattern said "Practise." They laugh, a little wildly, and say that is exactly what it said.

choices.text: Add a flower of your own

effects.log: You add a flower to the shelf, from your valley, and a label. {b3_rival} reads it twice.
You move the shelf into your own library, to be kept. It is a small and quiet theft.

events.text: Ten years on, the honey cakes become a tradition: every year at the feast of reconciliation, a tray appears on the border of your domain and {b3_rival}'s, and no one admits to baking them. Mortals leave offerings beside it.

choices.text: Leave a tray of your own

effects.log: You leave a tray of your own, with a note. The next morning, it is empty, and a feather rests on the cloth.
You wait and watch. At dawn, {b3_rival} arrives, in an apron, and stares at you like a deer.
You let the mystery stand. Some customs thrive only on being unclaimed.

events.text: Ten years on, the stone moved by the donkey, a little grey beast named Argument, is still at the foot of the mountain, and has become a pilgrim site. Visitors pat the donkey and ask for a blessing, and the donkey obliges, in the manner of its kind.

effects.log: You pat the donkey. It bites you, mildly. The pilgrims applaud, and {b3_rival} laughs so hard that they have to sit.

choices.text: Ask the donkey for a verdict

effects.log: You ask the donkey for a verdict. It sneezes, and the pilgrims interpret the sneeze as a victory for you.
You leave an apple. The donkey eats it and, in a rare moment of generosity, lets {b3_rival} do the same.

events.text: Ten years on, the priestess who praised {b3_rival} for the well has been to your shrine at last, and apologises with great ceremony for not knowing. She brings you a blue bowl full of well-water, and asks whether you will drink.

effects.log: You drink the water. It tastes of stone, and distance, and a faint, forgiving sweetness. She is crying a little.
You send the bowl to {b3_rival}. They drink from it, and return it with a leaf, and the bowl is never cold again.

choices.text: Tell her it makes no difference

effects.log: You tell her it makes no difference. She nods, unconvinced, and does not stop praying to you.

events.text: Ten years on, the crack in the wall of the world is a seam, and there is a pilgrimage to it, and tourists touch it for luck. {b3_rival} guards it in turns with you, and the guard-room has grown a stove, two chairs, and a shelf of the other's books.

effects.log: You add a third chair, for whoever might come by. The next week, a young god sits in it.
You leave a book on {b3_rival}'s shelf, with a bookmark. It is returned a month later with a better bookmark.
You seal the crack properly, with a ten-year work of stone and prayer, and {b3_rival} helps carry the final block.

events.text: Ten years on, {b3_rival} asks you again, in the middle of a feast, whether you ever think of the day you were nobody. This time they do not wait for your answer, but tell you theirs: a story of a rainy road, a cart, a stranger who gave them bread.

effects.log: You tell yours: a village, a bell, a girl who laughed. {b3_rival} listens without moving.

choices.text: Ask what happened to the stranger

effects.log: You ask what happened to the stranger. "I became a god," says {b3_rival}, "and they did not." The cup in their hand shakes.

choices.text: Raise a cup to the nobodies

effects.log: You raise a cup to the nobodies. The whole table follows, and the feast ends in a silence that is almost a prayer.

events.text: Ten years on, the inn on the pilgrim road has become your favourite, and you sit in its back room in disguise, enjoying the soup, which {b3_rival} wrote the recipe for in a rare burst of domesticity. The innkeeper is {b3_rival}'s oldest servant and has never told.

effects.log: You tell the innkeeper you know. He bows low, and brings a second bowl of the soup, free.
You ask {b3_rival} for the recipe. They send it, with a note of apology that is half a page long.
You keep eating in silence, as a loyal customer of a traitor. It is delicious.

events.text: Ten years on, the new Warden of the east sends for the two of you, and has grown into a grave and capable god. At the end of a long meeting, the Warden bows low and says: "I would like the two of you to come to the opening of the school. Together. It is the one wish I have."

effects.log: You agree at once, and {b3_rival} does too, and the Warden weeps behind a sleeve. The school opens with two chairs on the platform.

choices.text: Ask the Warden what they learned

effects.log: You ask what they learned from the two of you. "To keep both hands free," says the Warden, "and to be kind to enemies."
You decline, with regret, and {b3_rival} does not. The school is the better for the one chair filled.

events.text: Ten years on, the dance-duel has become the spring festival's centrepiece, and the nettle crown is an honour. {b3_rival} wears it two years running and carries it off. This year you decide to enter. They have already set a place for you on the floor.

effects.log: You dance with all you have. The Green Assembly roars, and the nettles sting, and you are crowned, stung across the brow.
You dance badly on purpose, and {b3_rival} dances worse out of kindness. The crowd laughs, and the crown goes to a child.
You refuse the dance and watch from the edge. {b3_rival} dances alone, to your music, and it is a quiet kind of victory.

events.text: {b3_rival} proposes a rite of the Green Assembly to decide who tends your domain: each of you will raise a grove from a single seed on a barren hill, and the faithful will judge by the harvest of prayers. The Assembly sends two seeds, in two plain boxes.

effects.log: You plant yours with care, and talk to it for a century. It grows crooked, and handsome, and the faithful come to sit in its shade.

choices.text: Swap the boxes in the night

effects.log: You swap the boxes in the night, for no reason you can defend. In the morning, you cannot tell which you took, and neither can they.
You plant yours beside theirs, in the same hole, which is against every rule of the rite, and which the Assembly is rather moved by.

events.text: A century on, the grove you raised is in full leaf, and the faithful have made a custom of it: a prayer tied to every branch. {b3_rival} comes to look, alone, at dusk, and touches the bark with the flat of a hand, and says: "It is a good tree. I will not pretend it is not."

effects.log: You offer them a branch to graft onto their own grove. They take it with an awkward, formal bow, and it takes root in the spring.
"Poorly," says {b3_rival}. "Lopsided. The faithful love it for that." You laugh together under your tree, and the dusk lengthens.
You thank them. They nod, and go, and in the morning there is a small offering at the foot of your tree in a hand you know.

events.text: A century on, the two seeds, one of which you swapped for the other, have grown into two groves, and the faithful cannot tell which is whose, and neither, honestly, can you. {b3_rival} stands at the border, bewildered, and says: "I have been tending your grove for a hundred years."

choices.text: Say that you have been tending theirs

effects.log: You tell them. They stare, and begin to laugh, a thin helpless laugh that goes on for a good while, and you laugh with them.

choices.text: Say that it is all one domain

effects.log: You say it is all one domain. They are quiet for a long time. The faithful, in the end, say the same.
You pretend you meant it. They narrow their eyes. It is the first time they have been out-schemed by an accident.

events.text: A dispute in the lower world over a river, which your domain says is yours and {b3_rival}'s says is theirs, has reached the point where two villages have drawn knives. The prayers arriving at both altars are the same prayer, from the same bank, in the same voice.

choices.text: Send a flood to part them

effects.log: You send a gentle flood. The two villages, up to their knees, stop shouting, and look at each other, and begin to pass buckets.

choices.text: Ask {b3_rival} to speak to the villages with you

effects.log: You send for {b3_rival}. They come, grim, and the two of you speak from the same cloud, and the villages hush, and stare.
You do nothing. It is a risk, and a cold one. The knives are put away by the villagers themselves, in the end, and you learn something about mortals and about yourself.

events.text: A decade on, the two villages have built a bridge over the river, and put a small shrine at its midpoint to "the god of both banks". You and {b3_rival} each visit it, separately, in disguise, on the same night, and meet on the bridge.

choices.text: Share a lamp at the shrine

effects.log: You share a lamp. The two of you stand on a bridge that mortals built, in the dark, and it is the most peaceful hour of the century.
You bow, and part. The shrine is left with two sets of footprints, and a bridge that hums.

choices.text: Argue about whose shrine it is

effects.log: You argue about whose shrine it is. It goes on for a decade. It is the happiest decade of the bridge.

events.text: A decade on, one of the two villages has fallen to blight, and the other has not. Prayers are rising from the stricken bank, pleading with whichever god will hear. {b3_rival} has already answered the blighted village in your name, and told no one.

effects.log: You complete it. The blight lifts. The mortals thank both gods, indiscriminately. {b3_rival} turns away at the thanks, as though stung.
You challenge them. "It needed doing," says {b3_rival}, stiffly, "and I did not want the credit." It is the worst-defended act of mercy in the heavens.
You leave them the credit, which they decline, and the mortals are left to guess, and guess, wrongly, kindly.

events.text: A young god of {b3_rival}'s court is caught stealing a prayer from your altar, a small, plain one, a mother asking for a child's fever to break. The young god is mortified. {b3_rival} brings them to you in person, by the ear, and offers an apology in the old formula.

effects.log: You accept. {b3_rival} is astonished, and the young god weeps, and the prayer is answered, and the matter becomes a small legend of the Silent Hall.
You demand a penance: a century of sweeping the steps of the lowest shrine. {b3_rival} says "Done" before the young god can speak.

choices.text: Say the prayer was never yours

effects.log: You say prayers belong to those who answer them, and the young god, hearing this, never steals another.

events.text: A century on, the young god who stole the prayer has become a quiet, respected servant of the lowest shrine, and comes to your altar, now and then, with a small offering. {b3_rival} watches this from afar with a look of deep, secret pride.

choices.text: Praise the young god in public

effects.log: You praise them in the court. {b3_rival} says nothing, and sends over a rare incense with a note that reads only "Hm."
You tell {b3_rival}. They say it was not them, and then, an hour later, in a lower voice, that it was, a little.

choices.text: Take the young god as a pupil

effects.log: You take them as a pupil. {b3_rival} is outraged, for a year, and then sends a gift.

events.text: A century on, the young god who stole the prayer is made to carry out your penance, a century of sweeping the lowest shrine, and emerges a harder, quieter thing. {b3_rival} notes it, and looks at you across the hall as at a person who has made a point.

effects.log: You nod. {b3_rival} nods back. The young god sweeps on, and the court does not know why the two of you seem to be at peace.

choices.text: Offer the young god a way out

effects.log: You offer the young god a way out, a seat in your court. They decline, politely, and keep sweeping, and it is somehow your loss.

choices.text: Say the penance was too long

effects.log: You say the penance was too long. {b3_rival} says it was exactly right. Neither of you is certain.

events.text: {b3_rival} sends you the oldest hymn to your domain, a thing of sixteen verses, found in a dead god's vault, and each verse names a different holder of the domain. The last is blank. A note: "I leave it to you to say who is next. Or to leave it blank."

choices.text: Fill it with your own name

effects.log: You write your own name in the last verse, in the old script. The ink does not take for a moment, and then it does.
You write theirs. It is the only verse in the hymn to bear a name of a living rival, and it takes the ink at once.
You leave it blank. The blank has a weight, and the hymn is sung with a pause, in every temple, ever after.

events.text: A century on, the hymn is sung at the turning of the age with the last verse unsung, and {b3_rival} stands at the back of the hall, listening to the pause. They look as if they had expected the silence to be longer, and are not sure whether to be relieved.

effects.log: You join them. The pause ends. The two of you stand there in a hall of gods who do not know what they have just heard.
You sing a verse, softly, of your own. It is not the verse. It is better, and the hall is very still.
You let it stand. The hymn goes on, with a pause, for a thousand years, and is called after the two of you.

events.text: A century on, the hymn has grown a new fashion: the faithful sing {b3_rival}'s name where the blank was, and your name before it, and think nothing of it. {b3_rival} is mortified, and moved, and cannot stop the singing.

effects.log: You let the mortals sing. {b3_rival} comes to your altar in a state of great confusion and sits, and says it is the nicest thing anyone has done to them.

choices.text: Ask the mortals to add a verse

effects.log: You ask for a verse for the pair of you. The mortals oblige, badly, and it is the most beloved hymn of the age.

choices.text: Step back, and let them have it

effects.log: You step back. The hymn is theirs, then, and it is sung, and in the end it stops being about either god.

events.text: Two worshippers, a farmer and a potter, have married across the border of your domain and {b3_rival}'s. Both gods are petitioned for a blessing. It is the first time in ten thousand years that both altars have been asked for the same thing, kindly, by the same mortals.

effects.log: You bless them, and send word. {b3_rival} blesses them, an hour later, with the same words, and a rather longer one.

choices.text: Bless them in secret, and say nothing

effects.log: You bless them in secret. {b3_rival} blesses them in secret. For a year, neither of you knows, and the couple is gloriously lucky.
You propose a joint blessing. {b3_rival} is silent for a day, and then arrives with a bundle of reeds and a very awkward bow.

events.text: A decade on, the farmer and the potter have a child, born with the sky in one eye and the soil in the other. It is a small, fierce, happy thing, and both altars have been asked to name it. {b3_rival} sends a messenger: "I will not name it without you."

effects.log: You name the child together, in a ceremony of the two courts, and the Silent Hall, for once, takes notes with visible warmth.
You let {b3_rival} name it. They choose something so sweet and so absurd that the child is called it for life, and is not ashamed.

choices.text: Name it yourself, in a rush

effects.log: You name it yourself. {b3_rival} is hurt, and then amused, and then sends a cradle, grudgingly, and a lullaby, not grudgingly at all.

events.text: A decade on, the quiet blessing has got out, and both altars are besieged by couples of the border, asking for the same, in the same words. The two courts are in uproar. {b3_rival} sends a note: "We have started something. I do not recommend running away from it."

choices.text: Open a shared altar for the border

effects.log: You open a shared altar on the border, with {b3_rival}, in the weather of the two domains. The line of couples is a hundred years long.

choices.text: Insist it is a clerical matter

effects.log: You insist it is a clerical matter, and hand it to the ministers. They add four forms. The couples marry anyway.
You refuse. {b3_rival} blesses them all, tirelessly, and the border begins to belong to them, and you find you mind less than you expected.
